title: F3D-01: Pin complete upstream/package; census every feature, registration, import, workflow and test
description:
## What this epic delivers

The immutable foundation of every later compatibility, ownership, and performance claim: a pinned Three.js r186 oracle, a pinned toolchain/dependency set, and the **single exhaustive feature manifest** (`compatibility/three-r186.json`) that records one entry per importable symbol and behavior family in the pinned release. Plan §19 lists this as F3D-01 with no dependencies; its acceptance evidence is "full source-to-feature reconciliation; unknown entries block; actual host/dependency matrix".

## Why it exists (plan §2.2, §5.11, §5.15, §14.1, §18 Phase 0, §21)

- The project promises **all existing features and functionality of r186**, not a convenient subset. That promise is meaningless until the complete surface is enumerated from the actual source tree, package exports, AST class/prototype surfaces, registration code (glTF extensions, nodes, codecs), editor/devtools/TSL tools, and official examples. A finite list in the plan document is explicitly *not* authoritative; the source is.
- The tag-object hash (`819fadd6...`) is **not** the source commit. The compatibility anchor is the commit `148ef33ecb6d2502ff796d4554abd1549c95d519`. Confusing them corrupts every later parity claim.
- The plan's release rule keeps import/symbol closure, validated behavior families, new-backend rendering coverage, exact-component integration, and capable-host validation as **separate** numbers. The manifest is where those numbers live. It is one generated JSON data file inside existing tooling, never a service, dashboard, or policy framework (AGENTS.md RULE 0.1).
- Section 21 says the first session begins by "recording the pinned Three.js commit and inspecting the complete source/package/feature/test map". This epic is that map.

## Children

1. Pin r186 oracle checkout and reconcile package metadata with built contents
2. Toolchain/workspace bootstrap: dated nightly, wasm32, pinned dependency set, budget method
3. Symbol/export census generator for compatibility/three-r186.json
4. Upstream test inventory and test-to-symbol mapping
5. Feature-family reconciliation and host/dependency matrix
6. Headline corpus H1-H8 and fidelity/control set closure; frozen benchmark corpus manifest v1
7. Examples/editor/Inspector/devtools/TSL-tool workflow inventory and crosswalk
8. Test evidence conventions and tiny shared logging helper (JSON-lines schema, evidence/ layout, owner/route tags)

## Success criteria for the epic

- Every child closed with its evidence in-tree.
- `compatibility/three-r186.json` regenerates deterministically from the pinned checkout; the generator fails on any unmatched source/export path.
- Counts are reported separately (symbols, families, tests, skips, unknowns). No "100%" is printed anywhere; the plan forbids labeling a census as implemented compatibility.

## No-claim boundary

A symbol census is not an implementation (AGENTS.md honesty rule 2). Nothing in this epic may be described as "supported", "compatible", or "accelerated".
acceptance_criteria: Full source-to-feature reconciliation of Three.js r186 (commit 148ef33ecb6d2502ff796d4554abd1549c95d519) exists as one generated manifest; every unknown entry is a blocking record; the actual host/dependency matrix and the frozen benchmark corpus manifest are committed. No implementation or acceleration is claimed by this epic.

title: Pin r186 oracle checkout and reconcile package metadata with built contents
description:
## Full scope

Pin the r186 oracle checkout and reconcile package metadata with built/package contents

## Summary

Establish the immutable upstream oracle: Three.js **r186**, release date September 8, 2026, source commit `148ef33ecb6d2502ff796d4554abd1549c95d519`. Record it, obtain it reproducibly, and prove that the package manifest describes files that actually exist.

## Background (plan §2.2, §5.11 item 1, §5.17, AGENTS.md "Upstream Pin Discipline")

Release updates are deliberate compatibility events, not automatic movements of the oracle. The annotated tag object (`819fadd6b663b74d828c6af72a543024f74d3877`) resolves to the source commit above; the two hashes must never be conflated. The plan also warns that "a manifest entry is not proof its file exists": package metadata (`exports`, `files`, wildcard addon/source paths) must be reconciled against the built package and the repository tree.

## Technical approach

- Add a small, documented procedure (script or Makefile target) that fetches the upstream repository at the exact commit into a clearly named oracle location (for example `upstream/three.js` as a git submodule pinned to the commit, or a documented shallow fetch), and verifies the checked-out HEAD equals the pinned commit. The oracle checkout is **never edited** (§14.2 uses a mapped working copy/resolver for tests).
- Record in a single committed file (for example `upstream/PIN.md` or a section of the manifest header): release name, release date, source commit, tag-object hash, package version string, and the date of inspection.
- Build the upstream package with its own pinned build scripts (`package.json` scripts, Rollup config) so that `build/three.module.js`, `build/three.webgpu.js`, `build/three.tsl.js`, `build/three.cjs`, and addon outputs exist locally.
- Reconcile: enumerate every `exports` entry (root ESM/CJS, `three/webgpu`, `three/tsl`, `three/addons`, wildcard `three/addons/*`, `three/src/*`), every `files` glob, and every packaged asset; verify the target files exist; emit a JSON discrepancy list (missing file, extra file, alias duplicates). Discrepancies are recorded, not silently dropped, because duplicates/aliases must be preserved as valid import paths (§5.11).
- Record the upstream toolchain requirements (Node version, package manager, Puppeteer/browser versions used by the E2E runner) as inputs for 01.4.

## Success criteria

- A fresh machine can reproduce the checkout and the reconciliation output byte-for-byte.
- The reconciliation JSON lists zero *unexplained* discrepancies; explained ones (for example intentional aliases) carry a reason.
- The pin file distinguishes tag hash vs source commit explicitly.

## Test plan

- Unit: `tools/upstream/verify_pin.test.mjs` asserts HEAD == pinned commit and that the tag-object hash is stored separately; reconciliation rule tests with a synthetic package.json (missing target, alias duplicate, wildcard path).
- E2E: a fresh-clone script (`scripts/oracle-checkout.sh --verify`) on a clean directory reproduces the checkout and the reconciliation JSON byte-for-byte; run in the functional lane.
- Logging: per-export-path lines `{step:"resolve", export, target, exists, reason}`; final summary with counts of resolved/explained/unexplained under `evidence/01.1/`.
- Failure artifacts: the discrepancy list and the offending `package.json` excerpt.

## Considerations

- Do not vendor a modified copy of upstream. Retained components used later (F3D-04) are pinned, isolated dependencies with their licenses; they are not edits of the oracle.
- Removed APIs from releases before r186 are not resurrected; still-shipped deprecated aliases and their warning behavior remain in scope and must appear in the reconciliation as valid paths.
- A newer upstream release must never be substituted here; a new target gets its own pin, manifests, and results (§5.17).
acceptance_criteria: A read-only pinned checkout of Three.js at commit 148ef33ecb6d2502ff796d4554abd1549c95d519 is reproducibly obtainable; package.json exports, built files, and packaged assets are reconciled with a machine-readable list of discrepancies; the tag-object hash is recorded separately from the source commit.

title: Toolchain/workspace bootstrap: dated nightly, wasm32, pinned dependency set, budget method
description:
## Full scope

Toolchain and workspace bootstrap: dated nightly, wasm32 target, coherent pinned dependency set, budget accounting method

## Summary

Create the minimal, correct build foundation: one dated nightly toolchain, the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` target, the Cargo workspace, the `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` policy, and one coherent set of pinned dependency revisions. This is bootstrap, not a "forest of empty crates" (plan §21): a crate is added only when it receives its first real code.

## Background (plan §13.1, §13.3, §13.4, §17.2, §23; AGENTS.md "Toolchain", "Dependency Policy", "Planned Workspace Crates")

- The release contract uses a **dated nightly**, never a moving `nightly` tag; a new nightly is tested in a separate lane before moving the anchor.
- The plan's source register inspected Asupersync at commit `efa5798d139ae3e877e13b2b8b5108fc5fe1a625` and other sibling manifests at then-current default branches; it explicitly requires resolving all chosen dependencies "into one coherent set of immutable revisions rather than treating separately inspected files as a tested integration". Version skew between Asupersync and any sibling crate must be resolved before integration: two independently instantiated Asupersync versions are not "one runtime".
- Allowed dependencies are a small audited allowlist (§13.4). Forbidden in the execution core: Bevy, general `wgpu`, a new generic ECS, Tokio, mandatory Rayon, native C/C++ FFI, BLAS, Python.
- Budgets: 205k crate subtotal, 10k charged Asupersync work, 30k reserve, 245k ceiling; ~12k JS/TS; ~15k authored WGSL. One pinned, consistently applied line-count method including tests (§17.2).

## Technical approach

- `rust-toolchain.toml` with an explicit `nightly-YYYY-MM-DD` and `targets = ["wasm32-unknown-unknown"]`; Rust 2024 edition; workspace-level lints including `unsafe_code = "forbid"` for first-party semantic/numerical/compiler/scene/resource crates. The browser-binding boundary is a named external boundary, documented as such.
- Workspace `Cargo.toml` listing only crates that exist with real code at this point (expected: `f3d-core` from F3D-05 and whatever F3D-02 needs). Reserve names for the eleven planned crates in a comment; adding a twelfth crate requires explicit user approval.
- Dependency admission records (one short markdown table or JSON, checked in): for each candidate crate, exact revision, used API, `wasm32-unknown-unknown` compile result, transitive closure, unsafe/FFI boundary, initialization requirements, incremental Wasm bytes, runtime allocation cost, demonstrated benefit. Prefer `default-features = false`.
- Pin the JavaScript ingestion toolchain (Rollup ecosystem + Acorn-class parser) with a lockfile in a bounded `tools/` package; it is a build-time dependency, never part of the deployed Wasm.
- Pin Naga's revision and record that its GLSL frontend targets Vulkan GLSL, not a turnkey ESSL entrance (§9.4); the ESSL normalization work is first-party (F3D-15).
- Pin the line-count method: a single script (`tokei`/`cloc`-style with fixed configuration) reporting new Rust, new JS/TS, authored WGSL, generated code, retained upstream modules, tests/assets, third-party dependencies as separate categories (§13.5, §17.2). Report the forecast vs ceiling.
- Record the DSR/RCH commands from AGENTS.md as the verification entry points; note that browser/GPU work never runs on RCH.

## Success criteria

- `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and native `cargo check` pass for the workspace on the pinned nightly.
- `cargo tree` shows no forbidden crates; each direct dependency has an admission record.
- The Asupersync revision selected here is the one used by F3D-02 and F3D-05; any needed sibling crate is on a matching Asupersync version or not used.
- Line-count script runs and prints all categories (initially near zero) without error.

## Test plan

- Unit: a workspace lint test that fails if any crate outside the named binding boundary lacks `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; a dependency-allowlist test that fails for a direct dependency without an admission record; a line-count script self-test on a fixture tree with known counts per category.
- E2E: `cargo check` native and `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` on the pinned nightly via the documented DSR/RCH commands; the run log is archived.
- Logging: toolchain/dependency resolution report `{crate, revision, features, wasm_ok, unsafe_boundary}` per dependency; line-count table by category under `evidence/01.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: `cargo tree` output and the exact failing command with its stderr.

## Considerations

- Do not add `simd128` flags globally yet; F3D-06 decides SIMD use per measured crossover with a scalar reference.
- Disk preflight (`sbh check --need 20G`) before heavy builds on this Mac (AGENTS.md).
- Keep this bead small. The plan's own warning: writing infrastructure before a single Rust future has been polled in a browser is the canonical failure.
acceptance_criteria: rust-toolchain.toml pins a dated nightly compatible with the selected Asupersync revision; the Cargo workspace exists with only the crates that receive real code in Phase 0; lockfiles and a single immutable dependency revision set (Asupersync, wasm-bindgen/js-sys/web-sys, serialization, Naga, Rollup-ecosystem + Acorn-class parser) are committed with per-dependency admission records; the line-count method is pinned.

title: Symbol/export census generator for compatibility/three-r186.json
description:
## Full scope

Symbol/export census generator producing the single feature manifest compatibility/three-r186.json

## Summary

Build the generator for the **one exhaustive feature manifest**, provisionally `compatibility/three-r186.json`: one record per importable symbol and its behavior families, expanded from the full recursive source/package tree, AST exports and class/prototype surfaces, documentation signatures, registered plugins/nodes/codecs, and official examples/tools.

## Background (plan §5.11, §5.15, §14.1, §14.10; AGENTS.md "THE NO-CUT RULE", RULE 0.1)

The plan's scope is the union of: (1) all package export paths and shipped public entry points; (2) every export, constructor, public method/property, constant, registration/extension hook, option, serialization contract and observable source-path utility in `src/` and `examples/jsm/` recursively (a module absent from `Addons.js` is *not* excluded); (3) all official backends, alternate renderers, controls, WebAudio/media, WebXR, physics wrappers, codecs and third-party integrations shipped or exercised by pinned examples; (4) editor/player, Inspector/devtools, TSL tools, examples and manual workflows as integration consumers.

`Three.WebGPU.js` exports backend classes, node builders, storage objects, render pipelines and loaders; those are part of the surface. The inspected `GLTFLoader` registers extensions beyond what documentation lists, so **registration code, not docs bullets**, is the source of truth for plugins.

AGENTS.md is explicit: the manifest is one generated JSON data file inside existing tooling. Do not build a service, dashboard, or validator-for-a-validator around it.

## Record schema (from §5.15)

Each record carries: immutable source path + blob identity; export aliases (every valid import path that reaches it); class/method/property/options and defaults; sync/async return contract; events/errors and state effects; serialization and extension behavior; **owner route** (new Rust / general new backend / retained JS / exact backend / unresolved); supported host prerequisites; implementation and behavioral-test references; functional status; new-WebGPU-path status; explicitly intrinsic native-backend dependency (if any).

Blocking statuses: `unclassified`, `unimplemented`, `untested`, `known-regression`, `stub`, `no-op-substitute`, `candidate-refusal-on-valid-source`. `retained` is ownership, not a pass. `host-blocked` requires the reference to share the missing prerequisite.

## Technical approach

- Implement the census as a Node script in the pinned `tools/` package using the pinned Acorn-class parser (already admitted for ingestion): parse every module, collect ESM exports (named/default/re-exports/namespace), CommonJS build exports, class declarations with prototype methods/getters/setters/static members, top-level constants, and `register*`/plugin/extension registration calls (`GLTFLoader.register`, node registrations via `addMethodChaining`/`registerNode`-style helpers, codec registrations). Resolve directory trees completely; "truncated/paged results cannot establish the census".
- Cross-reference documentation signatures (`docs/`) and TypeScript declarations (`types/` if present in the pinned tree) as additional evidence columns, never as the sole source.
- Initial status for every record: `unclassified`. Owner route: `unresolved`. This is honest; later beads (F3D-04, F3D-18a/b) update statuses with test references.
- Emit deterministic ordering and stable IDs (source path + export name). Print counts: total symbols, per-root counts, per-family counts (filled by 01.5), unclassified count.
- Add a "drift check" mode that re-runs the census and fails if new/unmatched entries appear versus the committed manifest (§5.17, §14.10).

## Success criteria

- Every export reachable through any documented entry point appears exactly once as a record, with all aliases attached.
- Running the generator twice yields identical output.
- The generator refuses to complete with any entry it cannot classify by source location (it reports them; the manifest still records them as `unclassified`).
- No percentage or "coverage" summary is printed as a single number.

## Test plan

- Unit: parser fixtures (re-exports, wildcard paths, class getters/statics, registration calls, CJS build exports) asserting exact records; determinism test (two runs, identical bytes); drift-mode test with an injected new export that must be reported.
- E2E: full census over the pinned checkout in the functional lane; spot-check assertions from the plan (`three/webgpu` exports backend classes; `WebGLXRFallback` present; `Addons.js` is not the sole addon entry).
- Logging: per-file parse events `{file, exports, classes, registrations, parse_ms}`; parse failures logged at `error` and fail the run; summary counts by root path and status (`unclassified` expected at this stage) under `evidence/01.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: list of unmatched/unparsed files with spans.

## Considerations

- Keep the manifest format simple enough to diff in code review; it will be large. Consider one JSON file plus a generated compact index if needed, but not multiple services.
- Do not attempt behavioral classification here; that is F3D-18. This bead only makes the surface complete and immutable.
acceptance_criteria: A deterministic generator walks the complete pinned source/package tree (src/, examples/jsm/, Three.WebGPU.js, Addons.js, wildcard paths, editor/devtools/TSL tools) and emits one record per importable symbol with the §5.15 fields; the build fails on unmatched or truncated entries; separate counters are printed for import/symbol closure and behavior families.

title: Upstream test inventory and test-to-symbol mapping
description:
## Full scope

Upstream test inventory: core unit, addon unit, E2E, WebGPU screenshot, tree-shaking; counts and test-to-symbol mapping

## Summary

Inventory the **complete** pinned test suite so later beads can run unchanged assertions against the candidate and so that the manifest knows which symbols upstream tests exercise (and which it does not).

## Background (plan §2.4, §14.1, §14.3, §14.4, §14.6; AGENTS.md "Upstream suite")

The pinned `package.json` distinguishes core unit tests, addon unit tests, end-to-end screenshots, WebGPU screenshots, and tree-shaking checks. Unit tests import individual source files (see `test/unit/three.source.unit.js`), including renderer-internal utilities like `WebGLRenderLists`; redirecting only the package name `three` will not redirect them. The E2E runner (`test/e2e/puppeteer.js`) excludes numerous difficult examples, selects a software Vulkan ICD, uses special launch flags, and applies a per-pixel rule plus a 0.1% different-pixel limit. That lane is a regression oracle, never a performance lane.

The plan requires counting active assertions, imported tests, TODO/skips, setup/import failures, host-blocked cases and newly written feature tests **separately**, and forbids claiming totals or a completion percentage before running the census.

## Technical approach

- Enumerate test files per lane from the pinned scripts: `test/unit/**` (core + addons registries), `test/e2e/**`, WebGPU screenshot list, tree-shaking check inputs.
- For each unit test module: record the module path, its import specifiers (exact source paths), the QUnit module/test names, a static assertion-count estimate, and any `todo`/`skip` markers.
- For E2E: record the example list, the exclusion list with upstream's stated reasons, the expected-screenshot assets, launch flags, ICD selection, thresholds. Preserve these verbatim; F3D-18a reuses them.
- Map each test module to manifest records by import path and by referenced class names; record symbols with **no** upstream test (this list is the seed for the plan's mandatory positive tests beyond upstream).
- Emit `compatibility/upstream-tests-r186.json` (or a section within the manifest) with per-category counts.

## Success criteria

- Every test file in the pinned tree is accounted for in exactly one lane, or explicitly listed as unused by upstream scripts.
- The unit-test import list demonstrates why package-name redirection alone is insufficient (a concrete list of src-level imports).
- Output includes: number of test modules, number of tests, estimated assertions, TODO/skip counts, E2E included/excluded counts, WebGPU screenshot count. No merged percentage.

## Test plan

- Unit: inventory fixture with one `todo`, one `skip`, two tests and a src-level import; assert lane assignment, counts and the import list.
- E2E: inventory over the pinned test tree; consistency check that every test-referenced source path exists in the manifest (a miss fails the run and points at 01.3).
- Logging: per-test-module events `{module, lane, tests, est_assertions, todo, skip, imports}`; summary by lane; the list of symbols with no upstream test written to `evidence/01.4/untested-symbols.json`.
- Failure artifacts: unresolved import paths with file/line.

## Considerations

- Do not run the suites here; this is inventory. Execution against the candidate is F3D-18a.
- Upstream skips remain visible as "unproven upstream case" later; they never become passes.
acceptance_criteria: Every active upstream test module is inventoried with its environment, import paths (including src-level imports), assertion counts, TODO/skips, E2E exclusions and the runner's launch configuration and thresholds; each test is mapped to manifest records; totals are reported by category with no aggregate percentage.

title: Feature-family reconciliation and host/dependency matrix
description:
## Full scope

Feature-family reconciliation and host/dependency matrix (every manifest record mapped to a §5.12 family row)

## Summary

Attach every census record to a row of the plan's mandatory family-level work map (§5.12) and record the real host prerequisites, inherited third-party dependencies, and intrinsic native-backend contracts per family. This produces the "actual host/dependency matrix" named in F3D-01's acceptance evidence.

## Background (plan §5.12, §5.13, §5.14, §18 Phase 0, §20 "Scope boundaries are not feature exclusions")

The §5.12 table is "the mandatory family-level work map, not a finite whitelist"; every source entry discovered under §5.11 must map to a row or add a row before release. Families include: package/module APIs; math and numeric helpers; scene graph and core data; geometry and attributes; curves/shapes/modifiers; cameras/views/output; animation and deformation; materials and render state; physical shading and color; lights/environments/shadows; textures and media sources; WebGL renderer contract; modern renderer/backend APIs; TSL/nodes/compute; legacy and dynamic shaders; postprocessing and effects; model/geometry/scientific loaders; texture/image and compression loaders; glTF and material extensions; exporters and serialization; controls and interaction; alternate renderers; audio and live media; WebXR/AR/VR; miscellaneous addons and physics integrations; Inspector/tooling/editor workflows; deployment/workers/environment behavior.

Each family row also fixes its **default implementation path and proof obligations** (for example "exact retained native GL where required", "new WebGPU implementation of standard execution", "retain full loaders/runtime dependencies").

## Technical approach

- Add a `family` field to each manifest record, assigned by path rules first (for example `src/math/**` → math; `examples/jsm/loaders/**` → loaders) and then by manual review for exceptions (for example `GLBufferAttribute` belongs to geometry/attributes but carries an exact-GL requirement).
- For each family, record: default owner route from the table; proof obligations; inherited external dependencies actually referenced by the pinned code (Draco/Basis/meshopt decoders, Ammo/Jolt/Rapier wrappers, KTX2 transcoder, OpenCascade/other example integrations), each with version and license; host prerequisites (secure context, WebGPU, WebGL2, WebXR device, WebAudio activation, SharedArrayBuffer isolation, file input, network); and concrete intrinsic native-backend contracts (real GL context, sync readback, native program handles, construction-time XR fallback).
- Emit the host/dependency matrix as a table in the manifest (or adjacent JSON) and a human-readable markdown rendering for review.
- Any record that cannot be mapped is recorded with `family: unmapped` and counted as blocking.

## Success criteria

- Zero `unmapped` records at close, or each remaining one has an open bead to add its row.
- The matrix names, for every family, the reference's real prerequisites, so that later `host-blocked` statuses can be verified against the reference (the plan forbids `host-blocked` where the reference does not share the missing prerequisite).
- The inherited-dependency list is complete enough that F3D-10/F3D-19 can decide runtime codec inclusion by dependency closure.

## Test plan

- Unit: path-to-family rule tests (src/math → math; examples/jsm/loaders → loaders; GLBufferAttribute → geometry with exact-GL requirement); a rule that `unmapped` counts as blocking.
- E2E: full reconciliation run; assertion that the plan's named examples land in the expected rows (retroreflection → physical shading; BundleGroup/QuadMesh/CanvasTarget → modern renderer APIs; WebGLXRFallback → XR).
- Logging: per-record `{id, family, owner_default, prerequisites, inherited_deps}`; per-family counts and prerequisite summary; `unmapped` list at `error` level under `evidence/01.5/`.
- Failure artifacts: the unmapped list with source paths.

## Considerations

- "Retained" means a production implementation wired to coherent public objects and tested end to end, not a stub or test-only alias. Recording the default route here does not close any feature.
- Physics/engine wrappers keep the same engine version and solver semantics; this bead records those versions so later acceleration work cannot substitute an approximation.
acceptance_criteria: Every manifest record maps to exactly one mandatory feature-family row (or a newly added row with rationale); inherited external dependencies, host prerequisites, and concrete native-backend requirements are recorded per family; unknown/unmapped entries are listed as blocking.

title: Headline corpus H1-H8 and fidelity/control set closure; frozen benchmark corpus manifest v1
description:
## Full scope

Headline corpus H1–H8 and fidelity/control set: full source/asset dependency closure inventory and frozen benchmark corpus manifest v1

## Summary

Preregister and freeze the demonstration corpus **before** any candidate performance exists. Inventory the eight headline workloads and the additional fidelity/control cases down to the exact controls, shaders, assets and navigation each one reaches.

## The corpus (plan §15.2, §15.3, §15.4)

| ID | Example | Forces |
|---|---|---|
| H1 | `webgpu_performance_renderbundle` | existing `BundleGroup`s, 4,000 heterogeneous objects, `MeshToonNodeMaterial` colors, static/dynamic toggles, Inspector, **navigation-based backend selection incl. genuine WebGL** |
| H2 | `webgl_marchingcubes` | per-step procedural geometry, resolution/blob count/isolation/wall/floor controls, env-lit Standard default plus Lambert, Phong, texture/color and **four legacy ShaderMaterial variants** |
| H3 | `webgl_animation_multiple` | multiple animated assets with independent poses |
| H4 | `webgl_shadowmap_performance` | repeated scene/shadow work, many objects |
| H5 | `webgl_instancing_dynamic` | instanced geometry with dynamic instance data |
| H6 | `webgl_postprocessing_advanced` | multiple effects, render targets, pass ordering |
| H7 | `webgpu_skinning_instancing_individual` | compute skinning via storage buffers and custom TSL, per-instance skeleton/morph data, shadows |
| H8 | `webgpu_compute_particles_fluid` | MLS-MPM multi-kernel compute, atomic cell data, indirect dispatch, runtime particle counts (default 32,768; storage for 131,072) |

Fidelity/control set (scored separately, always published): `webgpu_vxgi_sponza` (VXGI + TAA + external model index), `webgpu_postprocessing_ssgi`, `webgpu_postprocessing_traa`, `webgl_loader_gltf_transmission`, `webgpu_loader_gltf_dispersion`, `webgl_clipping_stencil`, `webgpu_clipping_stencil`, `webgpu_compute_cloth`, `webgl_materials_video` (and the WebGPU video example), a minimal deliberately GPU-bound full-screen shader (**negative control**), and a small ordinary interactive scene (**fixed-overhead/startup control**).

## Why now (plan §15.1, §15.6, §16.6)

Selection cannot become cherry-picking. Phase 0 may correct an invalid or unavailable candidate with a written reason and an equivalent replacement; after the manifest is frozen, a slow or difficult case stays in its declared category, and any corpus revision creates a new benchmark version that retains old results. Fewer than six headline cases, or loss of either modern-compute category (H7/H8), blocks a broad launch claim.

## Technical approach

- For each case, produce a closure record: HTML entry, every imported module (through `three/addons/*` and relative paths), every asset URL including ones resolved through external indexes (Sponza), GUI/control definitions with their value ranges, material selector branches, backend/URL-parameter branches (H1 reloads the page for several settings), and any `import.meta.url`/`new URL` resolution.
- Record the unmodified default as the correctness case; define stress variants only via documented controls or one shared harness parameterization applied identically to baseline and candidate.
- Freeze `benchmarks/corpus-v1.toml` (the file `f3d bench ./benchmarks/headline.toml` will consume): case IDs, logical workload definitions, quality settings, default and stress parameters, the observation contract (which state/events/pixels are compared), and the equal preregistered weights per cell.
- Note per case the hypothesized bottleneck class from §15.2 as a hypothesis, explicitly not a measured diagnosis.

## Success criteria

- All eight headline cases and every listed control case have complete closure records; any unavailable case is replaced with a written rationale in the manifest before any candidate run.
- Manifest v1 is committed with a version stamp and a rule that future edits require a new version.
- H1's inventory explicitly lists both backend settings and the navigation behavior; H2's lists all material branches.

## Test plan

- Unit: manifest schema validation for `benchmarks/corpus-v1.toml` (case ids, weights sum, stress parameters present, observation contract fields).
- E2E: closure verification per case: load each example under request logging and assert the recorded asset/module set equals the observed request set (no unrecorded fetch); GUI enumeration script asserts every recorded control exists with its range; run on Chrome and Safari.
- Logging: per-case events `{case, modules, assets, bytes, controls, backend_modes, navigation_paths}`; unrecorded requests logged at `error` and fail the case; archived under `evidence/01.6/`.
- Failure artifacts: request log diff and the GUI enumeration dump.

## Considerations

- Never increase difficulty only on the baseline or lower quality only on FrankenThreeD.
- The negative control exists to catch false CPU-only speedup claims; it must remain in the published report even when it shows no gain.
acceptance_criteria: For each of H1–H8 and every §15.4 fidelity/control case, the complete source/module/asset closure, every control, material variant, backend mode, navigation/reload behavior, external asset index, and stress parameterization is inventoried; invalid candidates are corrected with a written reason before any candidate performance is known; the benchmark corpus manifest v1 is frozen and versioned.

title: Examples/editor/Inspector/devtools/TSL-tool workflow inventory and crosswalk
description:
## Full scope

Examples, editor, Inspector, devtools, TSL-tool and manual workflow inventory with crosswalk to feature families

## Summary

Complete the inventory of **integration consumers**: the full examples index (`examples/files.json`), the editor (`editor/js/Editor.js` and its state: scripting, history, loading/storage, XR, renderer changes, animation), the Inspector, devtools, TSL tooling, and documentation/manual examples. Produce the exhaustive feature-to-example/test crosswalk required by §5.15 and §15.5.

## Background (plan §2.9, §5.11 item 4, §5.14 "Editor/Inspector/devtools", §14.9, §15.5)

The repository contains an editor, devtools, TSL tooling, documentation/manual examples, and the tests/examples trees. Reusing these tools is smaller than replacing them, but integration and behavioral verification are mandatory. "Demanding does not mean comprehensive": a fluid demo may barely exercise animation events. The crosswalk shows which families no headline demo touches so targeted tests can be written (F3D-18b, F3D-21b).

## Technical approach

- Parse the pinned examples index and each example HTML for imported modules and used classes; attach the example IDs to manifest records (many-to-many).
- Walk the editor source to list commands/history entries, menus, loader integrations, script execution paths, player preview, export/publish targets, XR entry, storage (IndexedDB) usage, and renderer selection; record each as a workflow with the upstream code path.
- Inventory Inspector hooks/panels and devtools integration points as source-visible debug APIs (they are part of the surface and must keep working; F3D telemetry is a separate namespace).
- Inventory TSL tooling (transpiler/editor) entry points and their dependencies.
- Emit the crosswalk: for each family, which examples/workflows exercise it; flag families with zero coverage.

## Success criteria

- 100% of examples index entries are accounted for (this is an inventory count, not a compatibility claim).
- Editor workflows listed match the plan's enumeration: import/edit/undo-redo/serialize/script/player/export/publish/XR.
- Uncovered-family list produced and referenced by the test-closure beads.

## Test plan

- Unit: example-index parser fixture; editor command-list extractor fixture (a small synthetic editor module with two commands).
- E2E: inventory over `examples/files.json`, `editor/`, Inspector, devtools and TSL tooling; sample verification of five examples' module/class lists by hand-authored expectations.
- Logging: per-example `{example, modules, classes, families}` and per-workflow `{tool, workflow, code_path}` events; parse failures at `error` (they fail the run); crosswalk summary with uncovered families under `evidence/01.7/`.
- Failure artifacts: list of examples/workflows that failed to parse.

## Considerations

- Editor-authored script execution keeps its original host/security requirements; the engine's rule against introducing `eval` does not prohibit a source application's existing scripting feature (§5.14). Record this so no later bead "sanitizes" it away.
acceptance_criteria: Every entry in the pinned examples index, every editor/player workflow (import, edit, undo/redo, scripts, animation, persistence, player, export/publish, XR, renderer changes), Inspector/devtools panels and TSL tools are inventoried and crosswalked to manifest families; uncovered families are listed for targeted tests.

title: Test evidence conventions and tiny shared logging helper (JSON-lines schema, evidence/ layout, owner/route tags)
description:
## Full scope

Test evidence conventions and a tiny shared logging helper: one JSON-lines event schema for unit, integration and end-to-end tests in Rust and JavaScript; an `evidence/<bead>/` archive layout with per-run summaries and failure artifacts; owner/route tagging on every result; kept to a few dozen lines, never a framework.

## Summary

Before the first executable evidence exists (02.2), fix how every test in the project reports what it did, so that later lanes, gates and audits can be read by humans and agents without guessing. This is a convention plus a minimal helper, not infrastructure: AGENTS.md forbids building a harness for a harness.

## Background (AGENTS.md "Output Style", "Testing Policy"; plan §14.3, §14.5, §16.4, §22)

Every result must record its implementation owner (new Rust/WebGPU, general new backend, retained JS, exact component, unresolved) and, for rendering, the route that actually submitted. Measurements distinguish app time from wall time. Raw runs are preserved. Failures must show the wrong value, not just "mismatch". The plan's gates are decided from archived evidence, so the archive layout must be stable from the first test.

## Conventions (the deliverable)

- Event schema (one JSON object per line): `ts_wall` (ms, measurement clock), `ts_app` (logical/app clock when applicable), `lane` (`unit` | `integration` | `e2e-functional` | `e2e-forced-new-backend` | `e2e-exact` | `bench`), `bead` (bead id), `test` (name), `step`, `level` (`info` | `warn` | `error` | `metric`), `owner` (route owner), `route` (actual submission route when rendering), `browser` (`{name, version, os}` for browser lanes), `device_generation`/`scene_generation` when relevant, `msg`, `data` (free-form object, bounded size).
- Archive layout: `evidence/<bead-id>/<run-id>/events.jsonl`, `summary.json` (pass/fail per test with counts and the first failing event), `artifacts/` (screenshots, image diffs, traces, capability records, profiler exports). Benchmark runs additionally follow `benchmarks/protocol-v1` (03.6).
- Rust: a test-only `tracing` subscriber writing the schema to the run file; `cargo test` output stays human-readable, structured lines go to the file. JS: a ~30-line `evidence.mjs` helper used by the harness (03.1) and by every e2e script.
- Failure rule: a failing assertion logs both observed and expected values (or pixel coordinates and channel deltas for images) and attaches artifacts; never only a boolean.
- Bounded: production code never depends on this helper; per-frame renderer logging remains prohibited (§8.8).

## Success criteria

- The helper exists in Rust and JS with one shared schema document (`docs/test-evidence.md`); 02.2's first run produces a conforming `events.jsonl` and `summary.json`; a schema validation test rejects a malformed event.

## Test plan

- Unit: schema round-trip tests in Rust and JS; a validator test with a deliberately malformed event (missing `owner`) that must fail.
- E2E: 02.2 acts as the first consumer; its run directory is checked for the required files.
- Logging: the helper is the logging; its own tests emit events to `evidence/01.8/`.
- Failure artifacts: n/a beyond the validator's diagnostic message.

## Considerations

- Keep it tiny (target under 150 lines total across Rust and JS). If it grows, stop and ask (AGENTS.md checkpoint rule).
acceptance_criteria: One JSON-lines event schema and evidence/<bead>/<run>/ layout are documented and implemented as a tiny Rust test subscriber plus a ~30-line JS helper; every result carries owner and route tags; the first foundation run (02.2) produces conforming events and summary; the helper stays under ~150 lines and is never a production dependency.

title: F3D-02: Execute Rust futures through the Asupersync browser host (Safari and Chrome)
description:
## What this epic delivers

Executable proof that Asupersync can be the **sole async foundation** for FrankenThreeD in a browser. Plan §19 lists this as F3D-02 (depends on 01) with acceptance "actual task bodies, wakeups, cancellation/drain in Safari/Chrome". It is the first half of kill gate 1 (Foundation).

## Why it is on the critical path (plan §2.3, §11.1, §11.2, §16.7, §20; AGENTS.md "Asupersync Is The Only Async Foundation")

The inspected Asupersync browser documentation distinguishes the shipped JS/TS ownership and host-adapter boundary from full native-style Rust task execution: its documented ABI task-spawn allocates a task handle rather than accepting an arbitrary Rust future, and the Rust-authored browser bootstrap is characterized as a preview with a remaining host-services gap. "Passing a `cargo check` for Wasm, or closing an ownership ledger, is not equivalent to proving that browser tasks actually executed and drained."

The rules that follow:
- No Tokio, no alternative executor, no unstructured promise pool as a workaround.
- One application Wasm instance linking the admitted Asupersync core/host integration; never a separately instantiated browser-core runtime plus a second FrankenThreeD runtime with independent memories and ownership tables.
- Missing host functionality is implemented **upstream in Asupersync**, not forked inside FrankenThreeD. That work is charged to this project's 10,000-line foundation allocation; exceeding it requires using the reserve and reassessing viability before accidentally building a second runtime.
- Acceptance evidence is executable behavior, not the presence of a contract document.

## Children

1. Gap analysis of the Asupersync browser host and version-skew resolution.
2. Rust-authored browser program: polled futures, timers, host-turn wakeups, nonreentrant pump.
3. Cancellation, fetch cancellation, drain before teardown, no late publication, unsupported-host behavior.
4. Upstream Asupersync host-services contributions charged to the foundation budget.
5. Region granularity and priority policy for FrankenThreeD.

## Success criteria for the epic

All children closed; the evidence is a small checked-in browser test page plus recorded logs from installed Safari and Chrome on the physical target machines (not a bundled automation WebKit build; that is a separate environment per §12.1). The foundation gate bead consumes this evidence.

## No-claim boundary

This epic establishes execution, not performance. It makes no statement about frame throughput.
acceptance_criteria: A real Rust-authored browser program, linked against the admitted Asupersync core/host integration, demonstrates in installed Safari and Chrome: futures polled with observed results, timers and host-turn wakeups without native threads, a nonreentrant scheduler pump with bounded microtask bursts, cancellation delivered to running cooperative tasks, real fetch cancellation and cleanup, child tasks drained before region teardown, no late publication into a cancelled scene, and explicit behavior for unsupported hosts. Missing host pieces are implemented upstream in Asupersync and charged to the 10,000-line allocation.

title: Asupersync browser host gap analysis and version-skew resolution
description:
## Full scope

Asupersync browser host gap analysis, version-skew resolution, and upstream work plan

## Summary

Before writing a line of runtime code, determine exactly what the pinned Asupersync browser host provides and what is missing for real Rust task execution, and decide how each gap is closed upstream.

## Background (plan §2.3, §11.1, §11.2, §13.2, §13.3, §23 [S12]–[S15])

Inspected artifacts: the Asupersync README (structured concurrency, qualified adapter guarantees), `docs/wasm_browser_scheduler_semantics.md` (required host-turn behavior), `docs/WASM.md` (ownership-ledger vs task-execution scope), and `asupersync-browser-core/Cargo.toml` (existing wasm-bindgen/js-sys/web-sys and serialization boundary). Sibling numerical libraries reference **older** Asupersync versions; "two independently instantiated versions with different ownership types are not one runtime."

## Technical approach

- Read the pinned Asupersync browser scheduler contract and WASM docs at the revision fixed in 01.2. For each foundation requirement (futures polled; timers/host-turn wakeups without threads; nonreentrant pump and bounded microtask bursts; cancellation to running tasks; fetch cancellation and cleanup; child drain before region teardown; no late publication into cancelled/replaced scene; explicit unsupported-host behavior) record: what API exists, whether it accepts an arbitrary Rust future or only allocates a handle, what the host adapter does today, and what is missing.
- Confirm the binding family versions (wasm-bindgen/js-sys/web-sys) FrankenThreeD will share with Asupersync's boundary; document that reusing that boundary is preferred to inventing a second bridge (§13.4).
- Decide the single Wasm instance design: FrankenThreeD's application module links Asupersync core + host integration; enumerate the exported host hooks the JS side must provide (timer, microtask, rAF/host-turn, fetch abort, worker messaging if any).
- Produce the upstream work plan: for each gap, the target Asupersync module, the semantic contract to implement, a test to prove it, and a line estimate. Sum the estimates against 10,000 lines; flag if the sum exceeds the envelope.
- Resolve skew: if any sibling crate (FrankenNumPy/SciPy) is wanted later, note whether its Asupersync version matches; if not, it is not used until upstream aligns.

## Success criteria

- Gap table complete with no "unknown" rows.
- One Asupersync revision recorded in the workspace lockfile and in the dependency admission record.
- Upstream plan reviewed by the user before 02.4 begins if estimates exceed the envelope.

## Test plan

- Unit: `cargo check --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` of a skeleton crate depending on the pinned Asupersync browser-core (default-features = false); a test that the pinned Asupersync revision string in Cargo.lock equals the one recorded in the admission record.
- E2E: none (analysis bead); the gap table is reviewed against the pinned docs.
- Logging: the gap table itself (`docs/asupersync-browser-gap.md`) with a status column and, for each `present` claim, a pointer to the executable probe in 02.2/02.3 that will verify it; the estimate sum vs the 10,000-line allocation.
- Failure artifacts: n/a.

## Considerations

- An ownership ledger closing is not proof a browser callback stopped executing. Every "present" claim in the gap table must point at executable behavior or be marked "unverified".
- Keep this analysis to what F3D-02 needs; do not audit all of Asupersync.
acceptance_criteria: A written gap list maps each §11.2 foundation requirement to the current Asupersync browser host status (present, partial, missing) at the pinned revision; the Asupersync revision is fixed for the whole workspace; each missing piece has an upstream design note and an estimate charged against the 10,000-line allocation.

title: Rust-authored browser program: polled futures, timers, host-turn wakeups, nonreentrant pump
description:
## Full scope

Rust-authored browser program: futures actually polled, timers and host-turn wakeups without threads, nonreentrant pump with bounded microtask bursts

## Summary

The first real Rust code in the repository: a tiny browser program that proves Asupersync-driven task execution works on the actual targets. Plan §21: "Execute a real browser Rust future and cancellation path; address the host gap before adding renderer abstractions."

## Background (plan §11.2, §4.9, §11.3; AGENTS.md "Concrete anti-pattern")

The scheduler must respect the browser event loop: task/microtask ordering and run-to-completion (§23 [S35]). A cooperative runtime must not split originally synchronous work across turns (§4.9), so the pump must be nonreentrant and bound its microtask bursts, yielding to the host on a defined policy. This bead produces executable evidence, not a document.

## Technical approach

- Create the first runtime crate (`f3d-runtime`, or a temporary example binary inside it) with `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` outside the named binding boundary. Link the pinned Asupersync core and browser host integration in **one** Wasm instance.
- Implement the host hooks in a minimal static JS shim (no `eval`): microtask scheduling, `setTimeout`/timer wakeups, host-turn (`requestAnimationFrame`/`MessageChannel`-style) wakeups, and a pump entry point.
- Test tasks: (a) a future that awaits a timer three times and records timestamps; (b) a chain of futures communicating through Asupersync channels/joins whose observed output order is logged; (c) a task that yields per host turn 1,000 times and records that each poll happened on a distinct macrotask; (d) a reentrancy probe: a host callback that tries to invoke the pump while it is already running must be rejected or deferred, never nested; (e) a burst probe: schedule 10,000 microtask-ready wakeups and assert the pump processes at most the configured bound before yielding.
- Log every observation as structured lines (JSON per event: task id, event, host time) into a page buffer that the automation harness collects; also print a final summary.
- Run on: installed Safari on the M5 MacBook and the iPhone 17 Pro Max (via the physical device), installed Chrome on the M5 MacBook. Record browser/OS build strings.

## Success criteria

- All five probes pass on both browsers with logs archived under `evidence/foundation/`.
- No native thread, SharedArrayBuffer, or Atomics.wait is required (§11.6: the first product must work without shared-memory threads).
- Wasm builds with the pinned nightly; the JS shim is static source.
- `f3d-runtime/CONTRACT.md` is written before any other crate depends on `f3d-runtime` (AGENTS.md "Documentation and Contracts"): purpose and position in the dependency direction, public types and semantics, invariants, implementation ownership route, error model, determinism and numeric-fidelity class, cancellation behavior, unsafe boundary if any, feature flags, conformance tests, and no-claim boundaries.

## Test plan

- Unit: Rust tests for the pump's state machine (nonreentrancy flag, burst bound, wake-source ordering) using a fake host; JS unit tests for the static shim's timer/microtask/host-turn hooks.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/foundation/execution.mjs` loads the Wasm page in installed Safari (M5 and iPhone) and Chrome (M5), waits for completion and asserts the five probes (polled futures, timers, host-turn wakeups, reentrancy rejection, burst bound); browser/OS build strings captured.
- Logging: one event per task lifecycle step `{task, event: spawn|poll|wake|complete, source: timer|host-turn|microtask, ts_wall}`; probe summaries with counts and max burst; archived under `evidence/02.2/<browser>/`.
- Failure artifacts: the full event stream around the first violation and a console capture.

## Considerations

- If Asupersync's spawn only allocates a handle and cannot poll an arbitrary future (the inspected gap), this bead blocks on 02.4 for that piece; do not work around it with a hand-rolled executor in FrankenThreeD.
- Keep the shim tiny; it will be replaced by generated host code later (F3D-05/F3D-12a), but its semantics (nonreentrancy, bounded bursts) carry forward.
acceptance_criteria: A checked-in Wasm test page, built from Rust on the pinned nightly and linked against the admitted Asupersync core/host integration, runs in installed Safari and Chrome and logs observed results of real polled futures, timer-driven and host-turn-driven wakeups, and a pump that is provably nonreentrant with a bounded microtask burst per turn.

title: Cancellation, fetch abort, drain before teardown, no late publication, unsupported-host behavior
description:
## Full scope

Cancellation delivered to running tasks, real fetch cancellation and cleanup, child drain before region teardown, no late publication, explicit unsupported-host behavior

## Summary

Complete the foundation milestone's second half: **structured cancellation and cleanup** that behave the way the plan's later lifecycle rules assume (device loss, scene replacement, stale worker results, cancelled uploads).

## Background (plan §11.2, §11.4, §11.5, §14.7, §22 "The foundation is real")

"Cancellation is not rollback of issued effects." A cancelled job retains a drain obligation. No late publication into a cancelled or replaced scene. Tests must "cancel at every supported await/publication boundary". Explicit behavior for unsupported host contexts is required rather than a silent failure.

## Technical approach

- Cancellation to a running task: a cooperative loop that checks its cancellation token between bounded chunks; the test cancels from a host callback and asserts the task observes cancellation within one chunk and runs its cleanup exactly once.
- Fetch cancellation: start a fetch of a large resource served by the local test server with a throttle; cancel the owning task; assert the browser aborted the request (server sees a disconnect; `AbortSignal` fired) and the response body stream is released. Log bytes received before abort.
- Drain before teardown: spawn a region with N child tasks holding a counter; tear down the region; assert teardown completes only after all children have finished or been cancelled and drained, and the counter is consistent.
- No late publication: a child produces a value after an artificial delay; the region is cancelled/replaced before the value arrives; the value must be dropped with a logged "stale result discarded (generation mismatch)" event, and must not appear in the replacement region's state. This is the prototype of the plan's generation-checked publication rule (§6.5, §11.5).
- Unsupported host: run the page with a required capability disabled (for example no `requestAnimationFrame` in a worker context, or no fetch) and assert a defined error object and no hang.
- Honest bound: document that a cancellation check inside a synchronous kernel cannot promise a main-thread cancellation callback runs before the browser regains control (§4.9); log the observed latency instead.

## Success criteria

- Five new probes pass on both browsers with archived JSON logs.
- Cleanup counters demonstrate exactly-once cleanup; no leaked timers or fetches after teardown (verify via a post-teardown idle probe).

## Test plan

- Unit: Rust tests for cancellation propagation, region drain ordering and generation-checked publication using a fake host with controllable delays.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/foundation/cancellation.mjs` on Safari and Chrome with the local throttled server: cancel-in-loop, fetch abort (server observes disconnect), drain-before-teardown, stale-result rejection, unsupported-host outcome; plus a negative run with the generation check disabled that must fail.
- Logging: lifecycle events `{task, region, generation, event: spawn|cancel-requested|cancel-observed|cleanup|drained|discarded-stale, ts_wall}`; fetch abort logs bytes received; cancellation-latency samples as `metric` events; archived under `evidence/02.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: leaked-resource report from the post-teardown idle probe.

## Considerations

- These semantics are what F3D-22a (fault injection) and F3D-11.5 rely on; do not weaken them later for convenience.
- If upstream Asupersync lacks a piece (fetch abort integration, region drain), it is implemented in 02.4, not here.
acceptance_criteria: The foundation test page additionally proves, in installed Safari and Chrome: cancellation observed inside a running cooperative task; an in-flight fetch aborted with the browser request actually cancelled and resources released; a region's child tasks fully drained before teardown returns; a delayed result that arrives after its region was cancelled/replaced is never published; and a defined, logged outcome on a host lacking a required capability.

title: Upstream Asupersync host-services contributions (charged 10k-line allocation)
description:
## Full scope

Upstream Asupersync browser host-services contributions (charged to the 10,000-line foundation allocation)

## Summary

Do the actual host-services work in Asupersync so that a Rust future can execute, wake, cancel and drain in the browser. This is the only place FrankenThreeD is allowed to change async foundation semantics.

## Background (plan §2.3, §11.1, §11.2, §13.3, §17.1; AGENTS.md)

"Where the browser host-services seam is incomplete, implement the missing host in Asupersync rather than forking its semantics inside FrankenThreeD." "The proposed 10,000-line foundation allocation is a planning envelope, not proof that the gap fits. Exceeding it requires using the reserve and reassessing project viability before building a second runtime accidentally." "Reusable improvements belong upstream where reasonable, and project-required new work is charged to this project's budget."

## Technical approach

- Work from the 02.1 upstream plan. Likely items (verify against the gap table): accepting and polling arbitrary `'static` Rust futures through the browser bootstrap; timer and host-turn waker sources; a nonreentrant pump with a configurable microtask burst bound; region/scope drain integrated with browser cancellation; fetch abort integration through `AbortController`; explicit unsupported-host error surface.
- Implement with tests inside Asupersync's own browser test lane; keep changes aligned with its structured-concurrency model (regions, scopes, cancellation as a first-class outcome).
- Coordinate with the Asupersync repository owner (same user); if an upstream merge cannot happen immediately, pin a branch revision and record "pending upstream" in the admission record.
- Count lines with the project's pinned method and record them in the budget report as "charged Asupersync foundation work".

## Success criteria

- 02.2 and 02.3 pass using only the pinned Asupersync revision plus FrankenThreeD's static JS shim.
- No FrankenThreeD-local executor, scheduler, or task type exists.
- Budget line: consumed lines vs 10,000; if over, a short viability note is filed and the user is informed before continuing.

## Test plan

- Unit: upstream Asupersync unit and browser tests for each contribution (future polling, waker sources, pump bounds, region drain, fetch abort, unsupported-host error); FrankenThreeD side runs 02.2/02.3 as integration.
- E2E: 02.2 and 02.3 probes pass using only the pinned Asupersync revision and the static shim.
- Logging: upstream test output archived alongside the foundation evidence under `evidence/02.4/`; the budget line (lines consumed vs 10,000) recorded in the code-count report.
- Failure artifacts: upstream test logs.

## Considerations

- Do not transplant Asupersync source into this repository to hide dependency or line count (§13.3).
- Retained upstream/external integrations (application codec/physics Wasm) keep their own host scheduling; they are disclosed components, not competing executors (§11.1).
acceptance_criteria: Every gap from 02.1 needed by 02.2/02.3 is implemented in the Asupersync repository (or a pinned fork branch pending upstream merge is explicitly disclosed), with tests there; FrankenThreeD pins the resulting revision; the line count consumed is recorded against the 10,000-line allocation with a viability note if exceeded.

title: Region granularity and priority policy (never per-object tasks)
description:
## Full scope

Region granularity and priority policy for FrankenThreeD: session/scene/asset/shader/worker regions, never per-object tasks, measured bounds

## Summary

Fix the shape of asynchrony in FrankenThreeD before any renderer code exists, so that later beads never create "one task per object, triangle, uniform, or draw".

## Background (plan §11.3, §4.9; AGENTS.md "Asupersync Is The Only Async Foundation")

Regions belong at session, scene/view, asset-preparation, shader/pipeline-preparation and worker-job granularity. The per-frame path is predominantly synchronous batched work; budget checks or chunk yields obey §4.9 (a check does not create permission to interleave an originally synchronous operation). The priority policy "must preserve UI responsiveness and cancellation progress without starving ordinary asset work. It is an engineering policy with measured bounds, not a claim of real-time scheduling guarantees from a browser."

## Technical approach

- In `f3d-runtime`, define region types and their ownership: `SessionRegion` (owns device/session lifetime), `SceneRegion` (per scene/view; owns pending preparation for that scene generation), `AssetPrepRegion` (decode/transcode/preprocess jobs), `ShaderPrepRegion` (pipeline/variant compilation), `WorkerJobRegion` (bounded background work). Each carries a generation used by publication checks.
- Document the invariant: frame preparation and submission run synchronously inside a host-turn callback; they never await inside the hot path; asynchronous preparation publishes only at boundaries allowed by its source adapter (§6.3).
- Priority policy: small number of levels (UI/cancellation, scene-critical preparation, background asset work); measured bounds: maximum pump time per host turn, maximum consecutive background chunks before yielding, cancellation latency bound. These are configuration values with tests, not a scheduler research project.
- Starvation test: run heavy asset-prep chunks while cancelling a scene region repeatedly; assert cancellation latency stays within the configured bound and asset work still makes progress.

## Success criteria

- Region types and generation-tagged publication helper exist and are used by 02.3's probes.
- Policy bounds are recorded numbers with a test that fails when violated.

## Test plan

- Unit: Rust tests for region type invariants (child regions cannot outlive parents; generation increments on replacement) and for the policy bounds (pump time per turn, consecutive background chunks, cancellation latency) using a fake clock.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/foundation/starvation.mjs`: heavy asset-prep chunks plus repeated scene-region cancellation; asserts cancellation latency within the configured bound and asset progress above a floor; Safari and Chrome.
- Logging: per-turn `metric` events `{pump_ms, chunks, cancellations, latency_ms}` and a histogram summary; archived under `evidence/02.5/`.
- Failure artifacts: the turn timeline around the bound violation.

## Considerations

- SharedArrayBuffer/worker pools are a later isolated-deployment option (§11.6); this bead assumes the main thread or a single supported worker.
acceptance_criteria: A short design note plus code skeleton defines the region hierarchy (application session, scene/view lifetime, asset preparation, shader/pipeline preparation, long-running worker jobs), the rule that the per-frame numerical/render path is synchronous batched work outside task machinery, and a priority policy with measured bounds for UI responsiveness and cancellation progress; a test demonstrates asset work does not starve and cancellation still progresses under load.

title: F3D-03: Profile strong references and bridge alternatives
description:
## What this epic delivers

The strong, unbiased denominator and the bridge decision. Plan §19 F3D-03 depends on 01 (and the bridge measurement integrates 02). Acceptance evidence: "Reference-only H1/H2/H7/H8 and matched completed-work data". This epic feeds kill gate 2 (Bridge) and everything in §16.

## Why (plan §1.2, §1.3, §16.1–16.6, §16.7, §20 rows 1–2)

The central hypothesis (`speedup = 1 / ((1 - p) + p/k + h)`) means the project must know how much of the reference's critical path is actually removable before writing an engine. The first risk in §20 is "the fastest Three.js baseline already removes the available overhead"; its earliest decisive test is the H1 baseline decomposition. The second risk is that Wasm/JS transfer erases gains; its test is the bridge probes. Both are answered here, with references that are **strong on purpose**: R0 as authored, R1 under a frozen bounded optimization recipe, R2 an equivalent current Three.js WebGPU implementation, selected by reference-only calibration and frozen before scored runs.

Everything measured here must be "completed logical frames per wall-clock second in a bounded steady-state pipeline", never `queue.submit` time or a GPU-only kernel timer.

## Children

1. Shared deterministic harness (clock/random injection, real measurement clock, input scripting, checkpoints, overhead calibration).
2. Fair uncapped offscreen lane with completion acknowledgement on both APIs.
3. R0/R1/R2 reference configurations and frozen bounded R1 recipe; independent calibration.
4. Reference profiles and critical-path decomposition (thesis test).
5. Bridge alternative measurements on matched workloads.
6. Frozen performance protocol and absolute budgets.
7. Device matrix provisioning, capability record, reserved-device and thermal discipline.
8. Statistical analysis pipeline (paired runs, block bootstrap, log-space aggregation).

## Success criteria for the epic

All children closed; a single `benchmarks/protocol-v1.md` (with machine-readable settings) and `evidence/references/` directory exist; the bridge gate bead can be decided from the recorded data alone.

## No-claim boundary

Nothing here is a FrankenThreeD result. Reference numbers are published as reference numbers.
acceptance_criteria: Reference-only H1/H2/H7/H8 measurements exist on the physical strata with R0/R1/R2 configurations selected by independent calibration and frozen; the four bridge variants are measured on matched workloads with completed-work data; the full performance protocol and absolute startup/memory/tail budgets are frozen before any candidate performance is known.

title: Shared deterministic harness: injected app clock/random, real measurement clock, scripted inputs
description:
## Full scope

Shared deterministic harness: injected application clock and random source, separate real measurement clock, scripted inputs, frame/state checkpoints, overhead calibration

## Summary

Build the one instrumentation layer both sides share, so equivalence and throughput comparisons are fair and reproducible. "Same input source on both sides except for explicitly shared harness instrumentation" (§1.3).

## Background (plan §14.5, §16.2, §16.3, §16.4)

- Use deterministic application clocks and random sources supplied by a shared harness. Overriding `performance.now()` or the animation timestamp for the application must not replace the wall clock used to compute throughput; app time and measurement time remain distinct.
- Preserve seed consumption, timer/microtask behavior, and one update per logical frame. Capture sequences of frames and state observations, not only the first frame.
- Test pointer/mouse/touch, wheel/pinch, keyboard, resizing, control-panel changes, loading completion/error, animation transitions, picking, material changes, scene add/remove, disposal.
- Include acknowledgement overhead and a matched empty/light-work calibration to quantify harness overhead.

## Technical approach

- `tools/harness/` JS package: `installDeterministicClock(seed, stepMs)` patching only the application-visible sources (`performance.now` as seen by app code, `requestAnimationFrame` timestamps, `Date.now` where the app uses it, `Math.random` via a seeded PRNG) while keeping an unpatched `measure.now()`; the patch is applied identically to reference and candidate pages via the same script tag.
- Input scripting: JSON event scripts replayed at logical frame indices (not wall times) through real DOM events on the real target elements, preserving pointer capture and focus semantics; GUI (lil-gui/dat.gui) interactions performed through their DOM controls.
- Checkpoints: at configured logical frames, capture a small state observation (selected object matrices, material params, event counters) and optionally a pixel readback; readback frequency must be equal on both sides to avoid asymmetry (§16.3).
- Calibration: a trivial scene with the harness attached vs detached to measure the harness's own cost; recorded with every protocol run.
- Structured logging: JSON lines per checkpoint/event with logical frame index and both clocks.

## Success criteria

- Two runs of the reference with the same seed produce identical event/state traces (up to documented nondeterministic diagnostic counters).
- The harness cost is measured and reported for every device stratum.

## Test plan

- Unit: PRNG determinism and clock-stepping tests (JS); input-script parser tests; checkpoint serializer tests.
- E2E: replay an input script on an upstream example twice with the same seed and assert identical event/state traces; a calibration run (harness attached vs detached) on each stratum recording overhead.
- Logging: JSON-lines per checkpoint/event `{frame, ts_app, ts_wall, kind, state_hash, event}` (schema from 01.8); calibration results as `metric` events; archived under `evidence/03.1/<stratum>/`.
- Failure artifacts: the first diverging trace pair with the input step that preceded it.

## Considerations

- Diagnostic FPS/GPU counters may differ between sides; excluded diagnostic pixels are narrowly identified before testing, never broad masks (§14.5).
- Transient activation cannot be recreated by replaying an event after an await (§3.4); scripts must trigger activation-sensitive actions from real input events.
acceptance_criteria: A harness library (JS, shared verbatim by reference and candidate) provides deterministic application time and seeded randomness, a separate wall clock for throughput, scripted pointer/keyboard/wheel/resize/GUI inputs, periodic frame and state checkpoints, and a matched empty/light-work calibration run that quantifies harness overhead; it never overrides the wall clock used for scoring.

title: Fair uncapped offscreen lane with completion acks on WebGPU and WebGL2
description:
## Full scope

Fair uncapped offscreen lane: fixed logical time, two logical frames in flight, completion acknowledgement on WebGPU (onSubmittedWorkDone) and WebGL2 (fenceSync/clientWaitSync), validated against on-screen reference behavior

## Summary

Because displayed FPS is capped (two applications capped at 120 FPS cannot show 3×), the scored measure is **completed offscreen-frame throughput** in a bounded pipeline. This bead builds that lane correctly and fairly.

## Background (plan §16.2, §16.3, §23 [S49], [S50])

- Freeze a small work-in-flight limit, provisionally two logical frames. Each logical frame includes all source updates, passes and effects; persistent simulation/history state advances exactly once.
- WebGPU: record submission high-water marks and resolve bounded completion credits with `queue.onSubmittedWorkDone()` (it acknowledges a queue high-water mark, not a per-command-buffer fence).
- WebGL2 reference: insert `fenceSync`, flush, poll `clientWaitSync` with zero timeout while yielding to the host. Neither side busy-spins; never compare per-frame `gl.finish()` on the reference with a pipelined candidate.
- Validate the reference's offscreen harness against its original on-screen rendering first: switching a Three.js scene to a render target can change output/tone-mapping or resolve behavior; a faster but incomplete offscreen pipeline is not eligible.
- Start the clock before the first scored update after an initial drain; stop after the last scored GPU work completes. Device loss, validation error, or rejected completion invalidates the run as a failure.

## Technical approach

- Harness module providing `OffscreenLane` for both APIs: creates the offscreen target(s) with the case's declared dimensions/format/samples, drives `N` logical frames with the deterministic clock, maintains the credit window, and records per-frame submit/ack timestamps.
- For Three.js WebGL references: a thin wrapper that renders to a `WebGLRenderTarget` plus the fence-based ack, with a validation mode that compares offscreen vs canvas output at checkpoint frames (color-space-aware compare).
- For WebGPU references (R2, and later the candidate): ack via `onSubmittedWorkDone`; frames in flight limited by credits.
- Report: completed frames, elapsed measurement time, throughput, ack overhead, plus the on-screen pacing companion numbers (frame pacing, missed deadlines, input response, long tasks) from a separate on-screen run of the same case.

## Success criteria

- Reference offscreen output matches its on-screen output within the preregistered tolerance at all checkpoints for H1/H2/H7/H8.
- Credit window enforcement proven by a test that artificially delays acknowledgements and observes the lane blocking at two frames.

## Test plan

- Unit: credit-window accounting tests (blocks at two, releases on ack, terminal path on failure) in JS; WebGL2 fence polling state machine test.
- E2E: offscreen-vs-onscreen validation on H1/H2/H7/H8 references at checkpoints (color-space-aware compare); an artificial ack-delay test proving the lane blocks at two frames; run on Chrome and Safari.
- Logging: per-frame `{frame, submit_ts, ack_ts, credits, api}` and a summary with throughput, ack overhead and validation result; archived under `evidence/03.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: offscreen/onscreen image diffs; the credit timeline.

## Considerations

- "An offscreen win that violates the interaction budgets does not pass the product gate" (§16.3); the on-screen companion run is mandatory, not optional.
acceptance_criteria: Both reference and candidate can render the same logical state sequence offscreen with equivalent target dimensions/formats/samples/output conversion; work in flight is capped at two logical frames using real completion acknowledgements on both APIs without busy-spinning; the reference's offscreen output is validated equivalent to its on-screen rendering; throughput is computed as credited completed frames over elapsed wall time.

title: Reference configurations R0/R1/R2 for H1/H2/H7/H8, calibrated and frozen
description:
## Full scope

Reference configurations R0/R1/R2 for H1, H2, H7, H8: frozen bounded R1 recipe, equivalent WebGPU R2 where available, independent reference-only calibration and freeze

## Summary

Construct the strong reference and freeze it. The denominator cannot be cherry-picked later.

## Background (plan §1.3 item 4, §16.1, §15.3, §20 row 1; AGENTS.md "References")

- **R0**: the pinned application with shared harness instrumentation only.
- **R1**: a frozen, bounded recipe of documented precompilation, instancing/batching, render-bundle and resource-management optimizations; not an unlimited manual rewrite, replacement simulation, or hand-written FrankenThreeD-equivalent compiler. Preserve the declared object/state/control contract, not only pixels; collapsing source objects or changing custom instance IDs just to accelerate the reference is not automatically eligible.
- **R2**: an equivalent current Three.js WebGPU implementation preserving scene/materials, logical updates, effects, resolution, precision, inputs. Where no genuinely equivalent migration exists, record the missing reference; do not invent one.
- Select the strongest eligible configuration using independent reference-only calibration, then freeze. Do not take the fastest noisy trial among many. Publish R0 and every eligible configuration. Render bundles and upload-range coalescing are baseline capabilities, not FrankenThreeD inventions; the selected reference must not leave applicable optimizations disabled.
- H1 already defaults to bundles; both the enabled-bundle reference and a competent instanced/material-data reference belong in the comparison if they satisfy the full observation contract.

## Technical approach

- Write `benchmarks/r1-recipe-v1.md`: the enumerated, bounded list of permitted transformations (for example `renderer.compileAsync` warmup, `BundleGroup`, `InstancedMesh`/`BatchedMesh` where the observation contract allows, static geometry merge only when identities are not observed, texture/material sharing, `frustumCulled` settings) with the explicit rule for what is *not* allowed.
- For each case, author the R1 variant(s) and R2 variant(s) as separate files under `benchmarks/references/<case>/`, each with a diff against R0 and a checklist proving the observation contract is preserved (controls, events, identities).
- Calibration: run all eligible configurations on each stratum with the protocol's repeat count; pick the strongest by the preregistered rule (median throughput with confidence check); freeze the selection in `benchmarks/references/selection-v1.json`.
- Record "missing reference" explicitly for any case where an equivalent R2 is not possible (for example if a legacy `ShaderMaterial` variant of H2 has no equivalent node-material port that preserves its contract).

## Success criteria

- Every headline case has a frozen selected reference with source hash and settings.
- The equivalence checks for each R1/R2 against R0 pass (visual/state/control at checkpoints).
- No configuration is deleted after calibration; all are published with their numbers.

## Test plan

- Unit: recipe checklist validator (each R1 transformation is in the allowed list; diff against R0 recorded).
- E2E: equivalence runs of every R1/R2 variant against R0 via the harness with protocol tolerances; calibration batches per case per stratum with the preregistered repeat count; selection rule applied by the analysis script.
- Logging: per-variant events `{case, variant, stratum, throughput, ci_low, ci_high, equivalence: pass|fail}`; the frozen selection record with source hashes; archived under `evidence/03.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: equivalence diffs for any ineligible variant (kept and published, never deleted).

## Considerations

- Improvement to reference code later creates a new frozen comparison version, never selective replacement of favorable runs.
acceptance_criteria: For each of H1/H2/H7/H8: R0 (as authored plus harness), R1 (frozen bounded documented optimization recipe preserving the declared object/state/control contract), and R2 (equivalent current Three.js WebGPU implementation, or a recorded "missing reference" with reason) exist; the strongest eligible configuration per case is selected by reference-only calibration runs and frozen with source and settings before any candidate exists; all configurations are published.

title: Reference profiles and critical-path decomposition (thesis test)
description:
## Full scope

Reference profiles and critical-path decomposition for H1/H2/H7/H8 (test of the central performance hypothesis)

## Summary

Before writing an engine, measure where the strong reference actually spends its time, so the project can tell whether "removing questions from the frame loop" can plausibly reach 2×/3× on each case. This is the earliest decisive test for §20's first risk.

## Background (plan §1.2, §2.1, §15.3, §16.7 "Generalization gate", §16.8)
