- Legality inputs from 12a.2's effect analysis: does any shader (built-in, node, or ESSL) read `gl_InstanceID`/`instanceIndex`/`vertexIndex`? Does the object have callbacks with observable effects? Is the material shared with mutable per-object state (`onBeforeRender` sets uniforms)? Is picking (raycast) dependent on `instanceId`?
- Merge plan: candidate group → instance stream with a logical-ID remap table so any observed index is translated back to the source's logical value (for shaders that read the index, either provide the source value through a per-instance attribute or refuse to merge).
- Winding: objects with negative determinant get their own bucket with flipped front face.
- Callback execution: batching changes physical draws only; the runtime still invokes each object's callbacks in upstream order with the same arguments; a counterexample test counts and orders callbacks with and without batching.
- Refusal reporting: each refused merge records a reason and source span in the build report (§3.5).

## Success criteria

- H1 (originally non-instanced objects with distinct materials) merges legally where the contract permits and the report explains each refusal; picking IDs on an instanced test scene match upstream.
- Callback multiplicity/order test passes; negative-scale objects render with correct facing.

## Test plan

- Unit: property tests over synthetic scenes with random callback/index usage asserting merges happen iff the observation contract permits; ID remap tests; negative-determinant bucket tests; callback multiplicity/order counterexample with a mutation variant.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/grouping/instancing.mjs` in the forced lane on both browsers: H1 merges legally with every refusal explained in the report; picking IDs on an instanced test scene match upstream; a shader reading `instanceIndex` keeps source-visible values; negative-scale facing correct.
- Logging: merge decisions `{group, merged: bool, reason, span}`; callback-order traces; archived under `evidence/08.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: the report excerpt and the callback trace diff.

## Considerations

- Collapsing source objects to accelerate is only legal for the candidate when identities are unobservable; the same rule constrained the R1 reference (§15.3), so the comparison stays fair.
acceptance_criteria: Draws merge into instance streams or grouped plans only when the compiler proves the observation contract permits it; instance/vertex/face IDs observed by shaders or picking are preserved; negative-determinant objects go to a separate winding bucket; onBeforeRender/onAfterRender and material callbacks fire per logical object in upstream order regardless of physical merging; a counterexample test proves callbacks are neither erased nor reordered; unknown shader side effects or callback-dependent state disable batching for the affected objects.

title: Persistent material programs and bindings with async precompile and bounded cache
description:
## Full scope

Persistent material programs and bindings: shader-program identity separate from mutable uniform values, specialization on geometry layout/material features/render state/lighting configuration, asynchronous precompilation of common variants, bounded variant cache, bind group reuse until structural dependencies change

## Summary

Answer "which objects share a program" once, at build time where possible.

## Background (plan §8.2 "Persistent material programs", "Persistent bindings and bundles", §9.3, §9.5, §16.9)

"Specialize on geometry layout, material features, render state, and lighting configuration. Separate shader-program identity from mutable uniform values. Precompile common variants asynchronously and bound the variant cache." "Reuse bindings and legal render bundles until their structural dependencies change." Also: "A finite proven variant set may be emitted ahead of time. Otherwise include the necessary runtime compiler/construction path automatically when reachable."

## Technical approach

- Program key type in `f3d-shader`; the compiler's analysis (12a) enumerates the variant set reachable in the application (for H1/H2: the finite material/control branches); variants get emitted WGSL ahead of time and are compiled asynchronously during startup within the region policy (02.5).
- Runtime variant path: a variant not in the precompiled set compiles on demand (it is a measured interaction-tail cost, §9.5); cache budgeted and evicting (07.1).
- Bind group cache keyed by (layout, resource identities, offsets); invalidated by resource generation changes.
- Report: variant table with source spans of the branches that produced them.

## Success criteria

- H2's material selector switches produce zero recompiles after warmup (all branches precompiled); a synthetic unseen variant compiles at runtime and is logged as such.
- Uniform sweeps cause zero pipeline creations (07.7 counters).

## Test plan

- Unit: program-key derivation tests (uniform value changes do not change the key; layout/feature/state/lighting changes do); cache budget/eviction tests; variant-table generation test from a fixture application.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/programs/variants.mjs` on both browsers: H2 material-selector sweep after warmup causes zero recompiles; uniform sweeps cause zero pipeline creations (07.7 counters); a synthetic unseen variant compiles at runtime and is logged as such; startup precompile timeline recorded.
- Logging: variant compile events `{variant_key, source_spans, precompiled: bool, compile_ms}` (feed the cold-start report); per-frame pipeline-creation counters; archived under `evidence/08.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: the variant table and the counter timeline.

## Considerations

- Never keep rendering an old shader or placeholder while a variant compiles and report success (§9.5): the runtime must either block at the source's synchronous boundary or use the source's own async boundary.
acceptance_criteria: Program identity is a key over geometry layout, material feature set, render state and lighting configuration; uniform value changes never trigger recompilation; common variants precompile asynchronously (createRenderPipelineAsync) within a bounded cache; bind groups persist across frames until a bound resource identity/offset changes; the build report lists precompiled variants and any runtime-compiled ones.

title: Render bundles with a structural key, executeBundles invalidation, rebuild-cost measurement
description:
## Full scope

Render bundles with a structural contract: bundle key (device generation, pipeline/layout, attachment formats and sample count, depth/stencil compatibility, bound resource identities, offsets, recorded draw parameters), rebuild rules for changed bindings/dynamic offsets/ranges/counts, frame-ring variants, measured rebuild cost and avoidance where bundles lose, executeBundles state invalidation, bundle-then-direct regression

## Summary

Bundles done by the book. Upstream H1 already uses bundles; the candidate must use them at least as well and never incorrectly.

## Background (plan §8.2 "Bundle reuse has a structural contract", §6.4, §23 [S37]; AGENTS.md "Bundles reset render-pass state")

- "A bundle key includes the device generation, pipeline/layout, attachment formats and sample count, depth/stencil compatibility, bound resource identities, offsets, and recorded draw parameters. Changing data in an already bound buffer can be legal; changing a recorded binding, dynamic offset, geometry range, or draw count is not an arbitrary in-place patch to the bundle. Frame-ring variants must have matching recorded bindings or be rebuilt."
- "After `executeBundles`, invalidate the host adapter's cached render-pass bindings and pipeline state before issuing subsequent direct draws. The API clears that state, even for an empty bundle sequence."
- "Command buffers themselves are freshly encoded for submission; a submitted command buffer is not a reusable render bundle."

## Technical approach

- `f3d-gpu::bundles`: bundle records with the structural key; encoder emits `GPURenderBundleEncoder` recordings via the ABI; validity checked each frame against resource generations and recorded parameters.
- Frame ring: if per-frame slices are used for dynamic data, either bind a stable buffer with a dynamic offset recorded identically (offsets are part of the key, so the ring must be addressed through a stable binding plus an indirection that is legal) or rebuild; document the chosen approach and its cost.
- State invalidation: the adapter's pass-state cache is reset after any `executeBundles`, including empty lists.
- Measurement: per-device bundle record cost vs saved per-frame encode cost; a heuristic threshold with ablation toggle.

## Success criteria

- Bundle-then-direct regression (from 05.7) passes through this code path with distinct bindings; the empty-list variant passes.
- H1 bundle on/off toggle matches upstream's observable behavior; counters show bundles reused across frames when static.

## Test plan

- Unit: bundle-key derivation and invalidation tests (data change in a bound buffer keeps the bundle; binding/offset/range/count change rebuilds); frame-ring variant tests; adapter state-reset test after `executeBundles` including the empty list.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/bundles/*.mjs` in the forced lane on both browsers: bundle-then-direct regression with distinct bindings through this code path; H1 bundle toggle observable behavior equals upstream; counters show reuse across static frames; per-device rebuild-cost measurement recorded.
- Logging: bundle events `{bundle, event: build|reuse|invalidate, reason, record_ms}` and per-frame reuse counters; archived under `evidence/08.4/`.
- Failure artifacts: readbacks after the bundle/direct transition and the bundle key diff.

## Considerations

- Bundles must not retain an expired external video texture (§8.5); the key includes the external texture's per-frame identity, which forces exclusion of such draws from bundles.
acceptance_criteria: Static draw portions become render bundles keyed by the full structural key; changing data in an already bound buffer reuses the bundle, changing a recorded binding/dynamic offset/geometry range/draw count rebuilds it; frame-ring variants have matching recorded bindings or are rebuilt; after executeBundles the adapter invalidates cached pass state before direct draws (including the empty-list case); bundle rebuild cost is measured per device and bundles are disabled for buckets where they lose; H1's bundle toggle behaves as upstream.

title: Rendering-order legality and conservative opaque batching
description:
## Full scope

Rendering-order legality: transparency sorting and custom blending, renderOrder, equal-depth surfaces, stencil, clipping, custom depth behavior, side-effecting shaders and callbacks; conservative opaque-batching rules; adversarial order tests

## Summary

"Rendering order is semantic." The bucket planner must never reorder what upstream's observable order fixes.

## Background (plan §5.5, §8.5 "Preserve sorted transparency")

- "Transparency, stencil operations, depth behavior, clipping, feedback, and callbacks can make order observable. Grouping and pass scheduling must respect those dependencies. Opaque batching is not automatically legal either. Equal-depth surfaces, `renderOrder`, custom depth behavior, side-effecting shaders, and callbacks can expose changes. Use conservative legality rules and test adversarial examples."
- "Weighted blended order-independent transparency is not an equivalent replacement for arbitrary sorted alpha blending and is not the default."

## Technical approach

- Transcribe upstream's render list sorting (`painterSortStable`/`reversePainterSortStable`, `renderOrder`, `groupOrder`, program/material/z keys) into the ordering classes; buckets exist within an ordering class and never across a boundary that upstream's comparator makes observable.
- Legality rule for opaque reordering within a class: identical depth function/write/test state, no stencil ops, no blending, no `depthTest=false`, no equal-depth candidates with different colors (detected conservatively via bounds overlap + depth-equality risk), no side-effecting shaders (storage writes/atomics), no order-dependent callbacks; otherwise preserve exact order.
- Transparent objects: always upstream order; custom blending states preserved.
- Adversarial suite: coplanar quads with different colors and equal depth; `renderOrder` mutated per frame; stencil masks; clipping planes with `clipIntersection`; a shader writing to a storage buffer; `onBeforeRender` toggling visibility.

## Success criteria

- Pixel and callback-order equivalence with upstream across the adversarial suite on both browsers.

## Test plan

- Unit: ordering-class derivation tests transcribed from upstream's sort comparators (`painterSortStable`, `reversePainterSortStable`, `renderOrder`, `groupOrder`); legality-rule tests for opaque reordering (equal-depth risk, stencil, blending, side effects, callbacks disable it).
- E2E: `tests/e2e/order/adversarial.mjs` in the forced lane on both browsers: coplanar quads with equal depth, per-frame `renderOrder` mutation, stencil masks, clipping with `clipIntersection`, storage-writing shader, `onBeforeRender` visibility toggles; pixel and callback-order equality with upstream.
- Logging: ordering-class assignment per object in debug and the reorder decisions with reasons; archived under `evidence/08.5/`.
- Failure artifacts: pixel diffs and the draw-order trace.

## Considerations

- "A fused shader must preserve required intermediate quantization and sampling boundaries" (§5.5); no fusion here.
acceptance_criteria: Grouping and pass scheduling respect every dependency that can make order observable; opaque batching is applied only where the conservative legality rule proves equivalence; sorted transparency and custom blending are preserved (no weighted-blended OIT substitution); adversarial tests with equal depths, renderOrder changes, stencil/clip interplay and side-effecting shaders match upstream pixel output and callback order.

title: Portable indirect draw/dispatch strategy with capability fallbacks
description:
## Full scope

Portable indirect draw/dispatch strategy: portable indirect commands with fixed slots or compacted instance streams, zero-instance slot cost accounted, capability-checked indirect-first-instance with bucket-base fallback, no indirect-count/multi-draw or bindless assumptions, bounded material/texture tables with compatible formats

## Summary

GPU-side selection without assuming native-style capabilities.

## Background (plan §8.3, §2.6, §12.3)

"For GPU-selected work, use portable indirect draw/dispatch commands and fixed slots or compacted instance streams as appropriate. Do not require a universally available indirect-count or multi-draw API. A zero-instance indirect slot is a conservative option, but its submission/validation cost still counts. Optional indirect-first-instance behavior must be capability-checked; a bucket-base index or equivalent legal representation supplies the fallback. Texture arrays or material tables require compatible formats/layouts and bounded bindings; do not assume arbitrary bindless texture access." "The architecture should not depend on universal support for native-style multi-draw-indirect, arbitrary bindless resources, mesh shaders, ray-tracing hardware, or shared CPU/GPU memory."

## Technical approach

- Indirect args buffer records from the layout schema; a per-bucket indirect slot; compaction kernel (compute) for GPU culling (used by F3D-20.6) writing instance counts; fallback CPU-side counts.
- Capability record gating: `indirect-first-instance` feature → use `firstInstance`; else bucket-base uniform + instance index arithmetic in shaders.
- Material tables: storage-buffer material blocks indexed per instance; texture arrays only for compatible format/size groups; otherwise per-bucket bindings.
- Cost accounting: number of indirect slots submitted (including zero-instance) in the telemetry.

## Success criteria

- Both capability paths render identically on a test scene; counters show zero-instance slot counts; no use of unavailable APIs on any stratum's capability record.

## Test plan

- Unit: indirect-args record layout tests; capability-gating tests (feature present → `firstInstance`; absent → bucket-base fallback); compaction kernel unit test via a CPU reference.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/indirect/paths.mjs` renders a test scene identically under both capability paths (device profile toggled) on both browsers; counters show zero-instance slot counts; no unavailable API used on any stratum's capability record.
- Logging: chosen path per bucket `{bucket, path, slots, zero_instance_slots}`; archived under `evidence/08.6/`.
- Failure artifacts: pixel diffs between paths.

## Considerations

- Priority 2: needed for H7/H8 routes (F3D-16) and GPU culling, not for the first product gate.
acceptance_criteria: GPU-selected work uses portable indirect draw/dispatch with either fixed slots or compacted streams; optional indirect-first-instance behavior is capability-checked with a bucket-base fallback; zero-instance slots are costed in the plan; texture arrays/material tables use compatible formats and bounded bindings; no code path requires indirect-count, multi-draw, or arbitrary bindless access.

title: Extended red-A/blue-B regressions (compute, multi-camera, nested callbacks, two frames in flight)
description:
## Full scope

Extended red-A/blue-B regressions: compute uniforms, multiple cameras, nested render callbacks, two logical frames in flight

## Summary

The plan's explicit extensions of the core counterexample, now that buckets, slices and bundles exist.

## Background (plan §6.7, §14.8; AGENTS.md "Queue ordering is not command-recording ordering")

"Extend it to compute uniforms, multiple cameras, nested callbacks, and two logical frames in flight. The planner tracks per-use data versions, not just a last value per object per frame."

## Technical approach

- Compute: two dispatches sharing a uniform block with different values in one submission; readback both outputs.
- Multiple cameras: render the same scene with camera A then camera B (changing a shared material color between them) to two targets in one submission.
- Nested callbacks: `onBeforeRender` of an object triggers `renderer.render(otherScene, otherCamera, target)`; verify the outer draw's parameters are unaffected and both outputs correct.
- Two frames in flight: with the credit window at two, mutate a shared uniform each logical frame; assert frame N's output reflects N's value while N+1 is already encoded.
- Each with a "wrong implementation" toggle in test builds to prove detection.

## Success criteria

- Four named tests pass on both browsers; mutation checks fail as expected.

## Test plan

- Unit: none new (integrated regressions).
- E2E: four named tests in `tests/e2e/counterexamples/queue-*.mjs` (compute uniforms; multiple cameras in one submission; nested render from a callback; two logical frames in flight with per-frame uniform mutation) on both browsers, each with a `--wrong-impl` mutation variant that must fail; enabled in the forced lane and benchmark mode.
- Logging: observed vs expected per-target pixel values and per-use versions; archived under `evidence/08.7/`.
- Failure artifacts: target readbacks and the packet dump.

## Considerations

- These stay enabled in benchmark mode (they are part of the measured optimized path).
acceptance_criteria: The queue-write snapshot regression is extended to compute uniforms, multiple cameras rendering in one submission, nested render calls from callbacks, and two logical frames in flight; each variant passes and has a mutation check proving detection; all run in the forced lane and in benchmark mode.

title: F3D-09: Complete marching-cubes computation/attribute behavior (H2)
description:
## What this epic delivers

The H2 half of the first product gate's compute content. Plan §19 F3D-09 depends on 04 and 05; acceptance: "H2 geometry/normals/colors and every parameter/material variant".

## Why (plan §4.6, §7.7, §15.3, §2.7)

"Known procedural geometry addon → safe Rust kernel behind the same API contract." "Start procedural geometry with known addon implementations such as marching cubes. CPU Wasm execution offers an early route to improvements without changing CPU-visible geometry." H2 "calls its procedural update on each animation step and exposes resolution, blob count, isolation, and wall/floor controls... Its default material and every material-selector branch, including the four legacy ShaderMaterial variants, belong in the first product slice; the UI cannot be restricted to an easy shader after the fact."

## Children

1. Marching cubes safe-Rust kernel behind the same API.
2. Rebuilt-geometry attribute behavior and allocation/upload reduction with differential tests.
3. H2 complete material/control closure wiring.

## Success criteria for the epic

All children closed; H2's geometry output is bit-identical (within the f32 storage the addon already uses) to the upstream addon for scripted control sequences; the kernel is derived from the addon's source semantics, not selected by example filename.

## No-claim boundary

"Faster" is not claimed until F3D-11.4 measures it under the frozen protocol.
acceptance_criteria: The MarchingCubes addon's per-step computation runs as a safe Rust kernel behind the identical public API with identical CPU-visible geometry, normals, colors, topology, output order and bounds for every resolution/blob/isolation/wall/floor setting; rebuilt-geometry attribute behavior follows upstream upload semantics with reduced allocation/upload work; every H2 material selector branch, including the four legacy ShaderMaterial variants, remains reachable and correct.

title: MarchingCubes addon safe-Rust kernel behind the identical public API
description:
## Full scope

MarchingCubes addon safe-Rust kernel behind the identical public API: field updates, polygonization, normals and colors, resolution/isolation/blob/wall/floor controls; identical CPU-visible geometry, output order, topology and bounds; synchronous observations preserved

## Summary

The first "known addon → Rust kernel" lowering, done as a semantic port of the pinned source.

## Background (plan §4.6, §4.7, §7.7, §15.3, §23 [S29], [S40])

"The first kernel must be derived from source semantics, not selected by an example filename, benchmark flag, or a memorized input trace." "GPU generation is valuable only where output order, precision, topology, bounds, and synchronous observations can still satisfy the contract" (so this is a CPU/Wasm kernel).

## Technical approach

- Read the pinned `MarchingCubes.js` fully: field array layout (`field`, `normal_cache`, `palette`), `addBall`'s falloff math, `addPlaneX/Y/Z`, the `polygonize` triangle table and vertex interpolation (`VIntX/Y/Z`), the normal cache computation, color handling, `count`/`maxPolyCount` limits, `enableUvs`, `enableColors`, `isolation`, `resolution` changes (reallocation), draw range setting, and attribute `needsUpdate` behavior.
- Implement the same algorithms in safe Rust operating on packed `f32` fields/outputs that are the same typed arrays exposed publicly (ownership per 05.5: Wasm-owned field/output buffers with the public `Float32Array`s as views/materialized copies at the boundary; identity preserved).
- Recognition: the compiler (12a) recognizes the unmodified pinned addon by blob fingerprint and swaps the update path; a modified copy keeps retained JS (§4.7).
- Exact float behavior: the addon computes in JS doubles then stores into `Float32Array`; replicate the same expression order in f64 and store as f32 to keep bit identity; transcendental uses (if any) follow 06.1's differential policy.

## Success criteria

- Differential test: random control sequences (resolution ∈ {28, 40, 56, 80}, blobs, isolation, walls) produce byte-identical position/normal/color arrays and identical draw ranges vs upstream.
- Public API identity: `instanceof MarchingCubes`, properties enumerable as upstream, synchronous `update()` observation of results.

## Test plan

- Unit: differential tests vs a Node oracle running the pinned `MarchingCubes.js` over random control sequences (resolution in {28, 40, 56, 80}, blob counts, isolation, walls/floor, `enableUvs`/`enableColors`) asserting byte-identical position/normal/color/uv arrays and identical draw ranges; property tests over field operations (`addBall`, `addPlaneX/Y/Z`, `reset`); identity tests (`instanceof`, enumerable properties, synchronous `update()` results).
- E2E: `tests/e2e/h2/kernel.mjs` runs the addon through the routed build in the browser with the same sequences and compares to upstream; a modified-addon fixture stays on retained JS.
- Logging: per-update `metric` events `{resolution, polygons, kernel_ms}` (timings are not claims); first array mismatch logged with index and both values; archived under `evidence/09.1/`.
- Failure artifacts: the shrunk control sequence and array diffs.

## Considerations

- SIMD variants only after the scalar port is bit-identical (06.1 policy).
acceptance_criteria: A Rust kernel (in f3d-math/f3d-scene) reproduces the pinned examples/jsm/objects/MarchingCubes.js algorithms (addBall, addPlaneX/Y/Z, reset, update/polygonize, normal and color generation, enableUvs/enableColors, the draw-range and attribute update behavior) with identical output for any control sequence; the public MarchingCubes class keeps its identity, properties and synchronous behavior; unrecognized subclass modifications fall back to the retained JS implementation.

title: Rebuilt-geometry attribute behavior and allocation/upload reduction for H2
description:
## Full scope

Rebuilt-geometry attribute behavior for H2: draw ranges, versioned upload ranges, buffer residency reuse across per-step rebuilds, reduced allocation and upload work; differential tests against the upstream addon at the GPU-visible level

## Summary

Make H2's per-frame rebuild cheap without changing what the GPU sees.

## Background (plan §5.8, §15.2 H2 "reduced allocation/upload work", §6.6)

The candidate gain for H2 is "bulk safe-Rust geometry kernel and reduced allocation/upload work". The attribute-history rules (06.6) apply: the addon sets draw ranges and `needsUpdate` on its attributes each update; the candidate must follow the source's request behavior.

## Technical approach

- Wire the kernel's output buffers to the attribute history system: kernel writes bump CPU version; the addon's `needsUpdate`/draw-range calls set the request version and ranges; the uploader computes effective ranges per upstream coalescing (the WebGL path uploads the full buffer when `updateRanges` is empty and `needsUpdate` is set; replicate exactly what the pinned attributes code does for this addon's usage).
- Residency: the position/normal/color buffers keep their GPU allocation across updates (no per-frame allocation); resolution changes reallocate per upstream (new array identity).
- Counters: allocations per frame, upload bytes per frame from 07.7.

## Success criteria

- GPU readback of the vertex buffer after each scripted step equals upstream's uploaded bytes (obtained from a reference run with an instrumented `bufferSubData`).
- Zero GPU allocations per steady-state frame; upload bytes per frame equal upstream's effective range bytes (or fewer only where upstream also would not have uploaded).

## Test plan

- Unit: planner tests for the addon's request pattern (draw range set + `needsUpdate` per update) reproducing the pinned attributes code's effective ranges; residency reuse tests (no reallocation across updates; resolution change reallocates with new identity).
- E2E: `tests/e2e/h2/uploads.mjs` in the forced lane on both browsers: GPU readback after each scripted step equals the bytes uploaded by an instrumented upstream run; steady-state frames show zero GPU allocations and upload bytes equal to upstream's effective ranges.
- Logging: per-frame `{effective_ranges, bytes, allocations}`; the instrumented reference's `bufferSubData` log stored as a fixture; archived under `evidence/09.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: byte-range diffs.

## Considerations

- Do not "optimize" by uploading only changed triangles unless the source's request contract says those bytes are the requested ones (§5.8).
acceptance_criteria: Per-step geometry rebuilds reuse GPU residency and upload only the source-requested ranges per upstream semantics; the GPU-visible bytes and draw ranges equal upstream's at every checkpoint; allocation and upload counters show the reduction; no early upload of CPU edits that upstream would leave GPU-stale.

title: H2 complete material and control closure (incl. four legacy ShaderMaterial variants)
description:
## Full scope

H2 complete material and control closure: default environment-lit Standard, Lambert, Phong, texture/color branches, the four legacy ShaderMaterial variants, and every GUI control reachable and correct through the routed build

## Summary

The "no UI restriction after the fact" guarantee for H2.

## Background (plan §2.7, §15.3, §9.5, §23 [S40])

"H2 starts with an environment-lit Standard material and exposes Lambert, Phong, texture/color, and four legacy `ShaderMaterial` choices." "The UI cannot be restricted to an easy shader after the fact." "Never keep rendering an old shader, a placeholder, a simpler material or a constant node while reporting success."

## Technical approach

- From 01.6's H2 closure record, generate the control sweep script (harness input format, 03.1): each material option, each slider extreme and mid value, toggles.
- Run through the routed build in the forced new-backend lane; compare checkpoints (visual with 03.6 tolerances; state traces) against upstream.
- Verify the variant table (08.3) contains all material branches as precompiled and that the four legacy shaders come from the ESSL pipeline (15a.2) with no retained renderer submission (07.6).

## Success criteria

- All sweep steps pass on both browsers; report shows every branch's owner route as new-backend.

## Test plan

- Unit: sweep-script generation test from 01.6's H2 closure record (every material option and control extreme/mid value present).
- E2E: `tests/e2e/h2/sweep.mjs` in the forced-new-backend lane on Chrome and Safari through every material selector value (Standard with env, Lambert, Phong, texture/color, the four legacy ShaderMaterial variants) and every control; checkpoints compared to upstream with 03.6 tolerances; route assertion per step.
- Logging: per-step events `{control_state, owner, route, max_err}`; the precompiled variant table attached; archived under `evidence/09.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: reference/candidate/diff images per failing step.

## Considerations

- Any legacy shader variant that cannot be translated portably is a **new-backend coverage gap** that blocks the first product gate; it is not reclassified as legacy-only (§9.5).
acceptance_criteria: A scripted sweep through every H2 material selector value and every control (speed, numBlobs, resolution, isolation, floor, wallx, wallz, dummy toggles as present in the pinned source) renders through the new backend with equivalence checkpoints passing; no branch is removed, stubbed or routed to a placeholder shader; the build report lists the finite variant set as precompiled.

title: F3D-10: Full standalone plus networked/module packaging
description:
## What this epic delivers

The product's output form. Plan §19 F3D-10 depends on 04 and 07; acceptance: "Reachable modes/codecs embedded; native H1 switch/reload; live mode not falsified as offline".

## Why (plan §3.1, §10.1–10.6, §16.9, §22 "The product is real")

"Self-contained HTML as the primary deployment form for applications with a closable code/resource graph. Also provide normal networked/module output for live-data, external-service, runtime-import, and library use cases. A deployment limitation is reported as such, not relabeled as an unsupported Three.js feature." "A proof of unreachability may omit a component; an unobserved branch in a captured trace may not."

## Children

1. Asset manifest and virtual resource resolver
2. Standalone HTML packer: safe embedding, memory accounting, CSP publication
3. Networked/module deployment mode and the isolated accelerated profile
4. Strict closure diagnostics and sandboxed capture (index locking, limits, traversal rejection)
5. Packaging verification harness (no-subresource, navigation, H1 GL after reload, interaction sweep)
6. Build cache on complete semantic inputs, deterministic rebuilds, incremental build cost
7. Asset preprocessing legality and runtime codec inclusion policy
8. f3d CLI orchestration: build/serve/explain with deterministic text and JSON output
9. Build-tool frontend adapters: Rollup/Vite plugin and Node API as thin wrappers over the f3d compiler

## Success criteria for the epic

All children closed; H1 and H2 standalone artifacts pass the packaging verification harness on both browsers; byte and peak-memory numbers are reported per artifact and feed 03.6's budgets.

## No-claim boundary

"A single file is a packaging mode, not a universal deployment environment." HTTPS/localhost serving is required for WebGPU; `file://` is not promised.
acceptance_criteria: The compiler emits either one self-contained HTML (all reachable code, compatibility components, Wasm, WGSL, CSS/fonts, codecs, assets and notices embedded; no undeclared subresource fetch after document load) or a networked/module build preserving live behavior; H1's native backend switch and reload work in the standalone artifact; live-data applications are never falsified as offline; packaging verification, build caching and the first f3d CLI surface exist.

title: Asset manifest and virtual resource resolver
description:
## Full scope

Asset manifest and virtual resource resolver: logical URI, content hash, media type, source/license metadata and dependencies; preserved relative base paths, setPath/setResourcePath, URL modifiers, query/fragment behavior and new URL(..., import.meta.url); one explicit closure policy for code, CSS, workers, shader includes and model resources

## Summary

The resolver that lets embedding change physical URLs while preserving logical loader/resource identity.

## Background (plan §10.1, §5.7 last paragraph, §10.5)

"Resolve assets through a manifest containing logical URI, content hash, media type, source/license metadata, and dependencies. A small virtual-resource resolver preserves relative base paths, loader `setPath`/`setResourcePath`, URL modifiers, query/fragment behavior, and `new URL(..., import.meta.url)` as required by the source application. Code, CSS, worker, shader-include, and model-resource resolution use the same explicit closure policy. Rewriting every request to an unrelated blob URL without a logical identity map is insufficient."

## Technical approach

- Schema (Rust types in `f3d-assets`, serde for build-time JSON): `AssetRecord { logical_uri, hash, media_type, bytes_len, license, provenance, deps: [logical_uri], reachable_via: [source spans] }`.
- Discovery: from the ingested module graph (04.1) and the corpus closure records (01.6): static string URLs, template URLs with finite closure, `import.meta.url` resolutions, loader `setPath` bases; dynamic capture (10.4) supplies observed requests but cannot prove unreachability.
- Runtime resolver (static JS in the generated host code): intercepts `fetch`/`XMLHttpRequest`/`Image`/`Worker`/`Audio` creation used by the retained loaders **through the LoadingManager and loader APIs upstream already exposes** (`setURLModifier`), mapping logical URIs to embedded bytes (blob or data URLs created on demand and released) or to networked paths; preserves `?query#fragment` semantics that loaders inspect.
- Identity map available to the report and to `f3d explain`.

## Success criteria

- H1/H2/Sponza closures resolve every request; a resolver test replays each recorded request and gets the right bytes with the right media type.
- `setPath`/`setResourcePath`/URL-modifier tests from upstream loader tests pass through the resolver.
- `f3d-assets/CONTRACT.md` is written before any other crate depends on `f3d-assets` (AGENTS.md "Documentation and Contracts"): purpose and position in the dependency direction, public types and semantics, invariants, implementation ownership route, error model, determinism and numeric-fidelity class, cancellation behavior, unsafe boundary if any, feature flags, conformance tests, and no-claim boundaries.

## Test plan

- Unit: schema tests; resolution-rule tests (relative bases, `setPath`/`setResourcePath`, URL modifiers, `?query#fragment`, `import.meta.url`, worker/CSS/shader-include requests); identity-map tests (logical → physical, never an orphan blob URL).
- E2E: `tests/e2e/assets/resolver.mjs` replays every recorded request from the H1/H2/Sponza closures through the resolver in embedded and networked modes on both browsers and asserts bytes and media types; upstream loader tests exercising `setPath`/`setResourcePath`/`setURLModifier` pass through the resolver.
- Logging: per-request `{logical, physical, source, media_type, bytes}`; unresolved requests at `error`; archived under `evidence/10.1/`.
- Failure artifacts: the request diff.

## Considerations

- Some HTTP/cache observations are incompatible with a fully embedded build; report those as admission boundaries, not fabricated network behavior (§10.1).
acceptance_criteria: f3d-assets defines the asset manifest schema and a resolver that maps every request an application can make (loader paths, LoadingManager URL modifiers, import.meta.url-relative assets, worker scripts, CSS, shader includes) to a logical identity and embedded/networked physical location; requests are never rewritten to unrelated blob URLs without a logical identity map; the manifest carries hashes, media types, licenses and dependency edges.

title: Standalone HTML packer: safe embedding, memory accounting, CSP publication
description:
## Full scope

Standalone HTML packer: embed all reachable code, compatibility components, Wasm, WGSL, CSS/fonts, codecs, assets and notices; context-aware HTML/script encoding validated by reparsing; bounded-chunk base64 with memory accounting; no undeclared subresource fetch; download bytes and peak startup memory reported; CSP allowances published

## Summary

The single-file deliverable, packaged safely and measured honestly.

## Background (plan §10.3, §10.4, §3.1)

- "The precise guarantee is no undeclared code/asset/subresource fetch after each document load."
- "Base64 increases encoded size, and decoding can create transient copies. The packer should use bounded chunks and release intermediate references promptly, but must not assume that the browser immediately frees embedded document text... Report both download bytes and peak startup memory. Do not pretend an embedded binary automatically gets the same streaming-compilation path as a separately served Wasm response."
- "Serialize embedded data with a context-aware HTML/script encoder: a source string containing `</script>` or attacker-controlled markup must not terminate a generated element. Escaping data for JSON alone does not establish safe HTML embedding. Validate generated scripts by reparsing them."
- "Publish the required CSP allowances, including Wasm execution and any blob-worker/resource requirements."

## Technical approach

- `f3d-cli`/`f3d-assets` packer: assembles the output HTML from a template with static generated host JS, embedded module code (retained upstream modules, exact components, adapters) as inline module scripts or import-map data URLs preserving module identity, Wasm as base64 (chunked), WGSL as strings, assets as base64 with media types, CSS/fonts inline, third-party notices/licenses section.
- Encoder: escape `</script`, `<!--`, and U+2028/2029 inside script bodies; HTML-escape attribute contexts; a reparse validation step (using the pinned parser toolchain) that asserts the produced document parses into the expected element/script structure.
- Memory accounting: startup instrumentation measuring string sizes, decoded byte totals, Wasm memory, staging and GPU allocations (07.1 budgets); reported per artifact.
- Wasm instantiation from bytes with a note that streaming compilation is unavailable for embedded bytes; measure compile time as part of cold startup.
- CSP: emit the minimal directive set (`script-src` with hashes/nonces as needed, `wasm-unsafe-eval` or the applicable directive, `worker-src blob:` if blob workers are used) in the report and as an optional `<meta>`.

## Success criteria

- H1/H2 standalone artifacts load under a network deny-list with zero blocked requests; the injection fixture (`</script>` in a shader string) produces a valid document.
- Byte and memory reports produced; they seed 03.6's budgets.

## Test plan

- Unit: encoder tests (`</script`, `<!--`, U+2028/2029 inside script bodies; attribute contexts); reparse validation test; chunked base64 decoder tests; artifact composition accounting tests.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/packaging/standalone.mjs` loads H1/H2 artifacts under a deny-all network interceptor on Chrome and Safari (zero blocked requests needed); injection fixture (a shader string containing `</script>`) yields a valid document; startup memory accounting captured; encoder fuzz test in the tooling lane.
- Logging: artifact composition table `{category, bytes}` per build; startup `metric` events `{phase, bytes_decoded, wasm_pages, staging_bytes, gpu_bytes, ms}`; CSP directive set; archived under `evidence/10.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: the intercepted-request log and the reparse diagnostics.

## Considerations

- Base64 vs alternative encodings: measure; keep the simplest correct one.
- Use HTTPS/localhost for verification; `file://` is not a promise (§10.3).
acceptance_criteria: f3d build --standalone emits one HTML whose only network request after document load is none (verified), initializes Wasm from embedded bytes, encodes embedded data with a context-aware encoder that survives a source string containing </script> or attacker-controlled markup, decodes in bounded chunks releasing intermediates, and reports download bytes plus peak startup memory (HTML/source strings, decoded bytes, Wasm memory, staging, GPU) and the required CSP directives.

title: Networked/module deployment mode and the isolated accelerated profile
description:
## Full scope

Networked/module deployment mode and the isolated accelerated profile: preserved live fetch/HTTP behavior, external services, supported dynamic module resolution, media/permissions and library/Node consumption; isolated profile with verified response headers as an additive, separately measured mode

## Summary

The "full networked/module deployment" that makes live applications and library consumers first-class, not a workaround.

## Background (plan §3.1, §10.4, §10.5, §16.6 "Deployment")

"Full networked/module deployment: preserve live fetch/HTTP behavior, external services, supported dynamic module resolution, media/permissions, and library/Node consumption. Required when those source behaviors are inherently non-embeddable; this is a first-release product mode, not an unsupported-feature workaround. A deployment selector cannot claim an offline snapshot preserves a live service." "Isolated accelerated deployment: the same functionality with verified response headers and optional worker/shared-memory features. This is additive and separately measured; it cannot rescue the portable accelerated score."

## Technical approach

- Output layout: `dist/index.html`, module files preserving the original module graph (rewritten only for the routed entry points), Wasm as a separate `.wasm` (streaming compilation possible), assets as files, plus a manifest.
- Live behavior: the resolver (10.1) in networked mode passes through to real URLs with original headers/credentials; dynamic imports with unresolvable closure remain dynamic; media/permission flows untouched.
- Library mode: an npm-consumable package output for applications that import the routed `three` facade in their own bundler; Node consumption remains synchronous (04.2).
- Isolated profile: emits a header manifest (`Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy`, `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy`) and a verification step in `f3d serve`/verify that checks `crossOriginIsolated`; optional features gated on it; scored separately.
- Selector logic: the strict standalone build fails (10.4) on unclosable live behavior and the report recommends networked mode; the report never says "offline equivalent" for such apps.

## Success criteria

- A networked build of Sponza (external model index) preserves live fetch behavior; the H1 networked build behaves as upstream; a library build passes the Node import tests.
- Isolated-profile verification detects missing headers.

## Test plan

- Unit: output-layout tests (module graph preserved; only routed entry points rewritten); header-manifest generation tests; selector-logic tests (live-service app cannot be labeled offline).
- E2E: `tests/e2e/packaging/networked.mjs`: Sponza networked build preserves live fetch through the external index; H1 networked build matches upstream traces; library build passes the Node import tests; isolated-profile verification detects missing COOP/COEP headers with a local server toggling them.
- Logging: deployment report `{mode, reasons, headers_verified, crossOriginIsolated}`; per-request pass-through log; archived under `evidence/10.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: header dump and request log.

## Considerations

- Shared-memory worker execution needs isolation supplied by the host, not a meta tag (§10.3).
acceptance_criteria: f3d build --deployment networked emits a multi-file module build that preserves live network behavior, dynamic imports, media/permission flows and library consumption; the isolated accelerated profile adds verified cross-origin-isolation headers and optional worker/shared-memory features without changing functionality; the deployment selector refuses to label a live-service application as an offline equivalent.

title: Strict closure diagnostics and sandboxed capture (index locking, limits, traversal rejection)
description:
## Full scope

Strict closure diagnostics and safe capture: unresolved URL expressions and dynamic imports reported with spans, external model index locking (Sponza), asset-pack limits, path-traversal rejection, sandboxed dynamic capture without credentials or private-network access, captured code treated as untrusted

## Summary

Close the graph honestly and safely, or fail loudly.

## Background (plan §10.5, §10.6, §3.5)

"A strict standalone build fails when it cannot close the resource graph. It reports the unresolved URL expression or dynamic import rather than quietly retaining network dependencies. The Sponza example resolves a model through an external model index. The packer must lock and include the selected index/model dependencies, not leave a mutable branch URL in the output." "Bound recursive assets, compressed expansion, geometry dimensions, shader size, and allocations. Reject path traversal or resource references outside the declared project/allowlist. Dynamic capture is an isolated build step without developer credentials, default private-network access, or arbitrary install-script privileges. Captured application code is untrusted, not part of the compiler's authority."

## Technical approach

- Closure analysis in `f3d-compiler`: classify each URL expression (literal / finite / unresolvable) with spans; unresolvable → strict failure with a suggested fix and a note that networked mode is available (§3.5 "changes needed to unlock").
- External indexes: when a loader fetches an index then a model (Sponza), the capture step records the resolved chain; the packer pins the index content and the selected entries; a mutable branch URL left in output is a build failure.
- Limits: configurable maxima (asset count, total bytes, decompressed size, geometry vertex/index counts, shader source size) with clear errors.
- Sandboxed capture: run the application in a headless browser process with a network allowlist limited to the declared project origin(s), no cookies/credentials, private-network requests blocked; the capture output is data only.
- Path checks: canonicalize and verify every embedded file is inside the declared roots.

## Success criteria

- Fixture with a variable dynamic import fails strict mode with the right span; Sponza closes with the index locked; traversal fixture rejected; a private-network fetch in capture is blocked and reported.

## Test plan

- Unit: URL-expression classification tests (literal/finite/unresolvable with spans); limit tests (asset count/bytes/decompressed size/vertex counts/shader size); traversal rejection tests; index-locking test with a synthetic model index.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/packaging/strict.mjs`: a variable dynamic import fails strict mode with the right span and a networked-mode hint; Sponza closes with the index locked; a private-network fetch during sandboxed capture is blocked and reported; capture runs without cookies/credentials (asserted by the local server).
- Logging: closure report listing every reference `{expr, span, class, resolution}`; capture network log with dispositions; archived under `evidence/10.4/`.
- Failure artifacts: the closure report and the blocked-request log.

## Considerations

- "An unobserved branch in a captured trace may not [be omitted]" (§3.1): capture adds evidence of reachability, never proof of unreachability.
acceptance_criteria: A strict standalone build fails with precise source spans when it cannot close the resource graph; the Sponza-style external index is locked and its selected dependencies embedded; recursive assets, compressed expansion, geometry dimensions, shader size and allocations are bounded; references outside the declared project/allowlist are rejected; dynamic capture runs isolated without developer credentials, default private-network access or install-script privileges.

title: Packaging verification harness (no-subresource, navigation, H1 GL after reload, interaction sweep)
description:
## Full scope

Packaging verification harness: deny network after each document load, clear caches, execute the complete interaction script through every reachable mode, allow only the frozen HTML document on intentional navigation with content identity checks, H1 count/bundle navigation and genuine WebGL backend after navigation, loader success/error, file input, resize, material switches, disposal, reopen, packed hash and license verification

## Summary

Proof that the single file is really self-contained and really complete.

## Background (plan §10.6, §15.3 "H1's complete backend and navigation contract", §16.6 "Standalone validity")

"After delivering each document, deny network subresource/code/asset requests, clear incidental caches, and execute the complete application interaction script, including every reachable mode. When a control intentionally navigates, allow only the frozen HTML document request and verify its content identity; then reapply the no-subresource rule... Test H1's count/bundle navigation as well as continuous animation. Its genuine-WebGL backend request must create the source-correct exact backend after navigation and remains a required functional test. Only the separately scored accelerated run fixes the WebGPU setting."

## Technical approach

- Harness mode in the tooling package: launch the artifact under HTTPS/localhost; install request interception denying everything except the document itself; on navigation (query-string changes for H1) allow the document request only if its bytes hash-match the artifact; replay the interaction script from 01.6/03.1 for every reachable mode.
- Assertions: zero denied-and-needed requests (a blocked request that the app needed shows up as an error/trace divergence); exact-GL route asserted after H1's WebGL navigation (`expectNativeGL`); loader success and error paths (an intentionally missing asset must produce the source's error behavior, not a hang); file input via a scripted file; resize; material switches; `dispose()` then reopen.
- Verification of packed hashes vs manifest and presence of every license notice for embedded third-party/upstream code.

## Success criteria

- H1 and H2 standalone artifacts pass on Chrome and Safari; the report lists modes exercised.

## Test plan

- Unit: interceptor rule tests (document-only allowance on navigation with hash check; everything else denied).
- E2E: the harness itself: H1 and H2 standalone artifacts on Chrome and Safari under deny-all interception with cleared caches; full interaction script through every reachable mode; H1 navigation reload allowed only for the frozen document with content identity; `expectNativeGL` after the WebGL branch; loader success and error paths; file input; resize; material switches; dispose and reopen; packed hashes and license notices verified.
- Logging: every intercepted request with disposition `{url, allowed, reason, hash_match}`; per-mode results with owner/route; archived under `evidence/10.5/<artifact>/`.
- Failure artifacts: the denied-but-needed request list, screenshots and trace diffs.

## Considerations

- WebXR and permission-dependent behavior need capable, explicitly identified environments; they are not silently credited here (§10.6).
acceptance_criteria: For each standalone artifact, an automated run denies network subresource/code/asset requests, clears incidental caches, replays the full interaction script including every reachable mode, permits only the frozen HTML document request on intentional navigation and verifies its content identity, and checks H1's WebGL backend selection creates the exact GL component after navigation; hashes and licenses are verified; results are separate from any performance number.

title: Build cache on complete semantic inputs, deterministic rebuilds, incremental build cost
description:
## Full scope

Build cache keyed on complete semantic inputs, deterministic rebuild verification, content-addressed build units, and incremental build cost measurement (a color-only edit must not rebuild every generated kernel)

## Summary

Developer experience and cache correctness are product properties.

## Background (plan §10.6 last paragraph, §16.9)

"Cache build artifacts using the complete semantic inputs... A stale cache hit must not resurrect a different material program or incompatible Wasm layout. Verify deterministic rebuilds where the build inputs admit determinism." "Rebuilding every generated kernel for a color-only edit is a design regression even if the deployed frame is fast." "Use bounded per-application specialization and content-addressed build units inside the existing compiler, not a new build platform."

## Technical approach

- Cache key derivation in `f3d-cli`: hash of the module graph bundle (04.1), asset manifest hashes, compiler crate revision, pinned upstream commit, toolchain, target features, ABI/layout schema versions (05.2/05.3), shader options, admission profile.
- Content-addressed units: per-island kernel, per-variant WGSL, per-asset preprocessed blob.
- Determinism check: build twice, compare artifact hashes; document any nondeterministic inputs (timestamps) and remove them.
- Measurements: scripted edits (change a material color; change an update function) with timings of the incremental rebuild; reported in the DX section of the report.

## Success criteria

- Deterministic rebuild for H1/H2; stale-key negative test (bump the layout version, cache must miss); color-only edit rebuilds only the affected units.

## Test plan

- Unit: cache-key derivation tests (each semantic input changes the key; a layout-version bump misses); content-addressed unit tests.
- E2E: deterministic-rebuild check on H1/H2 (build twice, identical hashes); scripted-edit timing script (material color change rebuilds only material-variant units; update-function change rebuilds only its island; asset swap; control addition) with cache hit/miss logs.
- Logging: cache events `{unit, key, hit|miss, reason}` and per-stage timings `{stage, ms}`; archived under `evidence/10.6/`.
- Failure artifacts: the two artifact hash manifests on nondeterminism.

## Considerations

- Keep it inside the CLI; no daemon or build service.
acceptance_criteria: Build artifacts are cached by source/module and asset hashes, compiler and library revisions, target/toolchain/features, ABI/layout version, shader options and admission profile; a stale cache hit can never resurrect a different material program or incompatible Wasm layout; deterministic rebuilds are verified where inputs admit determinism; clean and incremental conversion times, Rust/Wasm and shader compile times, cache hit correctness, generated bytes and the latency of a common material/update edit are measured and reported.

title: Asset preprocessing legality and runtime codec inclusion policy
description:
## Full scope

Asset preprocessing legality and runtime codec inclusion policy: predecode/reorganize static data only when public observations stay correct, no synchronous-ification of asynchronous loader callbacks, byte deduplication without sharing mutable objects, automatic inclusion of runtime decoders/transcoders when a caller can supply unseen inputs

## Summary

Optimize assets without changing loader contracts, and never ship a "please preconvert your model" error.

## Background (plan §10.1, §10.2, §5.13)

- "Static model/texture data can be predecoded or reorganized when public observations remain correct. Preserve required source metadata and response shapes: a caller may request text/bytes, inspect a loader result, or construct a second instance independently. Deduplicating asset bytes must not accidentally share mutable scene objects, materials, animation state, or callback identities."
- "Preprocessing must not make an originally asynchronous loader callback unexpectedly synchronous."
- "Runtime decoding and transcoding are mandatory whenever a caller can provide previously unseen compressed models, textures, archives, or local files. Include the needed existing codec or a verified replacement automatically. A build-time-only decoder cannot satisfy that contract."
- "Do not substitute lossier textures or geometry... Use capability-selected embedded variants, an included runtime transcoder, or a justified equivalent representation; one compressed format is not assumed to cover every target."

## Technical approach

- Preprocessing passes in `f3d-assets` (build-time only): glTF binary consolidation, texture format variants per capability profile (with the original retained when the profile is unknown), mesh reordering only when identities/orders are unobservable (provable from the loader's public contract).
- Async preservation: the resolver returns data through the same promise/callback microtask structure the original fetch would use (at least one turn of asynchrony), preserving `onProgress`/`onLoad`/`onError` order.
- Dedupe: identical bytes share storage; loader outputs are constructed per call (upstream loaders already construct fresh objects from parsed data; verify per loader).
- Codec inclusion rule in the closure analysis: if any reachable path accepts external input (file input, URL parameter, drag/drop, network fetch of unknown assets), include the runtime decoder(s) of every loader reachable from that path; report their bytes separately (§13.5).

## Success criteria

- Tests: predecoded glTF yields loader results equal (deep semantic compare) to runtime parsing; async ordering test; dedupe identity test; codec inclusion test on an app with file input.

## Test plan

- Unit: preprocessing legality tests (predecoded glTF yields loader results deep-equal to runtime parsing; async ordering preserved with at least one turn of asynchrony; `onProgress`/`onLoad`/`onError` order); dedupe identity tests (two loads produce independent objects); codec-inclusion rule tests on a fixture app with file input.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/assets/preprocessing.mjs` on both browsers: preprocessed vs runtime-parsed scene semantic equality; a standalone artifact with file input loads an unseen KTX2/Draco asset because the codec was included.
- Logging: preprocessing decisions `{asset, pass, proof_ref}` and codec inclusion list with bytes; archived under `evidence/10.7/`.
- Failure artifacts: the semantic diff of loader results.

## Considerations

- Mipmaps, block edges, orientation, premultiplication, color conversion and samplers must survive any texture variant (§10.2).
acceptance_criteria: Static models/textures may be predecoded or reorganized only with a recorded proof that response shapes, loader results, metadata and independent-instance construction remain correct; originally asynchronous callbacks stay asynchronous with preserved causal order; deduplicated bytes never share mutable scene objects, materials, animation state or callback identities; the closure analysis includes the runtime codec (Draco/Basis/KTX2/meshopt and any other reachable decoder) whenever the application can receive previously unseen compressed inputs.

title: f3d CLI orchestration: build/serve/explain with deterministic text and JSON output
description:
## Full scope

f3d CLI orchestration (f3d-cli): build --compat full (default) with --standalone/--deployment networked, serve, explain; deterministic human text plus stable JSON output; --require-accelerated-webgpu diagnostic strict mode; inspect/verify/verify-upstream/bench subcommands accrue from their owning beads

## Summary

The thin orchestration layer (7,000-line budget) over the compiler, packer, and harness. Section 21 warns a polished CLI is not a substitute for a working artifact; this bead stays minimal and grows only as commands get real backends.

## Background (plan §3.2, §3.5, §17.1; AGENTS.md "Output Style")

```
f3d inspect ./src/main.ts --format json
f3d build ./index.html --compat full --standalone --out ./dist/demo.html
f3d build ./src/main.ts --compat full --deployment networked --out ./dist
f3d verify ./index.html --candidate ./dist/demo.html
f3d verify-upstream --ref r186 --features all --tests all
f3d bench ./benchmarks/headline.toml --device local
f3d explain ./dist/demo.f3d-report.json
f3d serve ./dist --port 8080
```
"`--compat full` is the default, not an optional premium or later phase. A developer may additionally request `--require-accelerated-webgpu`... That diagnostic strict mode fails if its acceleration requirement cannot be met; it does not redefine the full product's functional scope." "CLI output must be deterministic and documented, with stable JSON alongside human-readable text."

## Technical approach

- `f3d-cli` crate with a small argument parser (audited dependency or hand-rolled), subcommand dispatch to `f3d-compiler`/`f3d-assets`/`f3d-conformance` APIs; `serve` is a minimal static HTTPS/localhost server with optional isolation headers (10.3).
- `explain` renders the build report JSON (12a.9) as text.
- JSON envelopes with a schema version; exit codes documented.
- Native asset/build tooling never becomes a dependency of the deployed Wasm (§17.3).

## Application profiles (plan §3.2)

An application profile (the `--profile` input consumed by `build`, `verify` and `bench`) selects inputs, settings, permissions and performance workloads for a run. It **cannot** delete valid upstream API contracts or reachable controls from the full-compatibility claim: a profile that omits a control still ships that control's code and its compatibility components; only the strict `--require-accelerated-webgpu` diagnostic may fail a build, and only for an unmet acceleration requirement. The CLI rejects any profile field that would narrow functional scope and says so in the report.

## Success criteria

- `f3d build` produces H1/H2 artifacts; `f3d serve` serves them for the verification harness; `f3d explain` prints the report; JSON output validated against a schema in tests.
- `f3d-cli/CONTRACT.md` is written before any other crate depends on `f3d-cli` (AGENTS.md "Documentation and Contracts"): purpose and position in the dependency direction, public types and semantics, invariants, implementation ownership route, error model, determinism and numeric-fidelity class, cancellation behavior, unsafe boundary if any, feature flags, conformance tests, and no-claim boundaries.

## Test plan

- Unit: argument parsing and exit-code tests per subcommand; JSON envelope schema validation with snapshot tests of text output; profile validation tests (a profile field that would narrow functional scope is rejected with a message).
- E2E: `f3d build` produces H1/H2 artifacts; `f3d serve` serves them for the packaging harness; `f3d explain` prints the report; the `--require-accelerated-webgpu` strict mode fails only for an unmet acceleration requirement (fixture).
- Logging: structured stderr diagnostics (bounded) with stable codes; command timing `metric` events; archived under `evidence/10.8/`.
- Failure artifacts: the failing command line with stdout/stderr.

## Considerations

- Do not add commands without a backend; a stub subcommand is exactly the process-porn AGENTS.md forbids.
acceptance_criteria: The f3d binary exposes build/serve/explain with the proposed flags; --compat full is the default; --require-accelerated-webgpu fails only when an acceleration requirement is unmet and never narrows the functional artifact; every command emits deterministic text and stable JSON; errors are structured and actionable; inspect/verify/verify-upstream/bench are wired as they land in F3D-12a.9/F3D-18a.5/F3D-23.

title: Build-tool frontend adapters: Rollup/Vite plugin and Node API as thin wrappers over the f3d compiler
description:
## Full scope

Build-tool frontend adapters: a Rollup/Vite-family plugin and a small Node API that invoke the same `f3d` compiler (`build`, `verify`, `explain`) from an application's existing build, so ordinary bundler, module and Node-side utility integration are real delivery paths rather than a separate toolchain; the adapters are thin, pinned, audited, and never a dependency of the deployed Wasm.

## Summary

Plan §3.2: "Existing build tools are thin frontend adapters to the same compiler. Ordinary bundler, module, Node-side utility, and upstream editor/player integration are required delivery paths, not excuses to invent another language toolchain." F3D-10.3 provides the networked/library outputs; this bead provides the integration surface developers actually use to produce them from their own projects.

## Background (plan §3.2, §4.1, §10.4, §17.3)

The JS ingestion toolchain is already the pinned Rollup ecosystem plus an Acorn-class parser (04.1). A plugin that runs inside that ecosystem gives projects with existing Vite/Rollup builds a one-line integration: their build normalizes TypeScript/JSX, `f3d` ingests the normalized graph, and the plugin emits the full-compatibility artifact (standalone when closable, networked otherwise) plus the report. Native asset/build tooling must never become a dependency of the deployed Wasm (§17.3).

## Technical approach

- `tools/adapters/rollup-plugin-f3d` (works under Vite's Rollup pipeline) exposing `f3d({ mode: 'standalone' | 'networked', profile, requireAcceleratedWebGPU })`; it hands the bundler's resolved module graph to `f3d build` (10.8) and writes the artifact and `f3d-report.json` into the bundler's output directory; errors surface as bundler diagnostics with the same source spans as the CLI.
- Node API `@f3d/build` with `build()`, `verify()`, `explain()` wrappers over the CLI's JSON envelopes (no second implementation).
- Documentation examples for a plain HTML project, a Vite project and a library consumer; each is an integration test fixture.

## Success criteria

- H1 and H2 built through the plugin produce byte-identical artifacts to `f3d build` on the same inputs; a TypeScript Vite fixture builds end to end; diagnostics carry spans; the deployed Wasm has no dependency on the adapter package.

## Test plan

- Unit: plugin option validation; envelope wrapper tests against recorded CLI JSON; a dependency-graph test that the adapter is absent from the artifact.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/adapters/*.mjs` building the three fixtures through the plugin and running the packaging harness on the outputs on both browsers.
- Logging: plugin events `{fixture, mode, ms, artifact_hash}` and bundler diagnostics captured; archived under `evidence/10.9/`.
- Failure artifacts: bundler logs and artifact hash diffs.

## Considerations

- A modified `three` in the project's `node_modules` is routed as an unrecognized revision with truthful status (04.2); the plugin never silently swaps it.
acceptance_criteria: A pinned Rollup/Vite plugin and a Node API invoke the same f3d build/verify/explain with identical outputs to the CLI, surface diagnostics with source spans in the bundler, build a TypeScript Vite fixture end to end, and are never a dependency of the deployed Wasm.

title: F3D-11: First complete-application and new-backend product gate (H1 and H2, >=2x on phone and M5)
description:
## What this epic delivers

Kill gate 3. Plan §19 F3D-11 depends on 08, 09, 10, 12 (early), 15 (early), 22 (early); acceptance: "Full H1/H2 behavior and >=2× named new-backend phone/M5 results with actual full artifact".

## Why (plan §16.7 "First product gate", §18 Phase 1, §20 row 1)

"Automatically transform the complete H1 and H2 applications, preserve all controls/backend modes and material variants, and separately score H1's WebGPU dynamic workload plus H2 through the new renderer. Both H1 backend modes must work; retained exact execution cannot count as the new-backend speedup. Include actual guards, materialization, bootstrap, and bridge costs. Require the >=2× floor against the independently selected strong references on the phone and M5 strata before broad compatibility implementation proceeds. If H1 is not viable against its competent reference, do not replace it with an easier toy without explicitly reopening the project decision."

Phase 1 deliverables: "full H1/H2 output artifacts; every control/mode works; all guards, compatibility bytes and setup costs measured; independently validated new-backend phone/M5 speedups; no file-name/trace-specialized cheat." Exit: "first product performance gate and both applications' full functional tests pass. Exact H1 GL mode is not counted as accelerated; it is still implemented and tested."

## Children

1. H1 automatic end-to-end transformation.
2. H2 automatic end-to-end transformation.
3. H1/H2 equivalence validation.
4. Scored paired runs on the phone and M5 strata.
5. Kill gate 3 decision record.

## Success criteria for the epic

All children closed with the decision recorded. If the gate fails, this epic closes with a "failed gate" reason and the project decision is reopened by the user; Phase 2+ epics must not proceed as if it passed.

## No-claim boundary

Passing this gate is a result for two applications on two strata. It is not a universal claim and not the launch contract (§16.6, §22).
acceptance_criteria: The complete H1 and H2 applications are transformed automatically with every control, backend mode, navigation path and material variant intact; H1's WebGPU dynamic workload and H2 are scored through the new renderer with actual guards, materialization, bootstrap, bridge and compatibility bytes in the ordinary full artifact; paired runs against the frozen strong references on the iPhone 17 Pro Max and M5 strata meet the >=2x floor with 95% lower bounds; both applications' full functional tests pass; the kill-gate decision is recorded.

title: H1 automatic end-to-end transformation (all controls, both backends, navigation, Inspector)
description:
## Full scope

H1 automatic end-to-end transformation: original webgpu_performance_renderbundle source through the compiler to a full artifact with every control (static/dynamic, object count, bundle toggle, materials, camera controls, resize), both backend settings (WebGPU via new backend, WebGL via exact component), navigation/reload behavior, Inspector, and no file-name/trace specialization

## Summary

The first real product: H1, whole, automatic.

## Background (plan §2.7, §15.3, §4.7, §18 Phase 1, §21)

- "H1 already defaults to 4,000 objects, uses multiple geometry types and distinct toon-material colors, and supports render bundles and dynamic behavior. It is a particularly good test of whether the compiler can combine equivalent material programs and packed state without changing source-level identity."
- "The first compiler slice must already cover the guards, alias checks, input packing, output materialization, and conservative path required by the H1 update loop... the first kernel must be derived from source semantics, not selected by an example filename, benchmark flag, or a memorized input trace."
- H1's complete backend and navigation contract (§15.3): both source backend settings, static/dynamic updates, object counts, bundle settings, materials, camera controls, resizing; page reloads for several settings; WebGL choice produces a genuine GL-backed renderer.
- "Next connect the original H1 source to the candidate compatibility boundary, even before it is fast. Preserve object identity and its dynamic/control behavior." (§21)

## Technical approach

- Run the full pipeline: ingest (04.1) → routing (04.2/04.4) → semantic analysis and island extraction of H1's animation loop (12a.2–12a.5: per-object rotation/position updates driven by time → bulk kernel + packed `AffineRows` upload) → material program specialization (08.3) + legal grouping (08.2) + bundles (08.4) → pass graph/execution plan (07.2/07.4) → packaging (10.2) with the exact GL component embedded for the WebGL branch.
- Verify each control via the interaction script; verify navigation reload creates a fresh route decision; verify the Inspector.
- Anti-cheat: build a copy of H1 with renamed identifiers, reordered declarations and a different file name; the compiler must produce equivalent islands/plans (report diff) without any example-specific table.

## Success criteria

- All controls and both backends pass the packaging verification harness (10.5) on Chrome and Safari; the build report shows the islands, guards, groupings and the exact-GL route for the WebGL branch; the renamed-copy test passes.

## Test plan

- Unit: none new (end-to-end product bead); relies on the compiler and packaging unit suites.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/h1/full-artifact.mjs` on Chrome and Safari: packaging verification harness (10.5) over every control and both backend settings; navigation reload; Inspector operation; the anti-cheat renamed/reordered copy of H1 produces an equivalent report (islands, guards, groupings, routes) via `f3d inspect` diff; forced-new-backend lane equivalence at checkpoints.
- Logging: build report archived as evidence; harness events per control with owner/route; report-diff summary for the renamed copy; archived under `evidence/11.1/`.
- Failure artifacts: screenshots, trace diffs, both build reports.

## Considerations

- Do not narrow the artifact to the WebGPU branch to save bytes; the performance setting chooses what is measured, not what is shipped (§15.3).
acceptance_criteria: f3d build on the unmodified H1 source produces a standalone artifact in which all controls work, the WebGPU setting renders through the new backend with guarded update islands for the dynamic loop, the WebGL setting constructs a genuine GL renderer through the exact component after navigation, the Inspector operates, and the compiler's decisions are derived from source semantics (verified by transforming a renamed and lightly reordered copy of H1 with identical results).

title: H2 automatic end-to-end transformation (kernel, all materials, export/read after updates)
description:
## Full scope

H2 automatic end-to-end transformation: original webgl_marchingcubes source through the compiler to a full artifact with the marching-cubes kernel, every material branch including the four legacy ShaderMaterial variants, environment lighting, all controls, and current-state export/read observations after accelerated updates

## Summary

H2, whole, automatic, including the legacy shader branches that a "static shaders only" product would skip.

## Background (plan §15.3, §2.7, §5.13 "Export must work after an accelerated update", §18 Phase 1)

Phase 1: "Integrate marching cubes, legal batching/bundles, resource histories, standalone packaging and current-state export/read observations."

## Technical approach

- Pipeline as in 11.1; addon recognition (09.1) by pinned blob identity; ESSL variants via 15a.2; env-lit Standard via 07.3.
- Observation tests after accelerated updates: read `geometry.attributes.position.array` values post-update; `mesh.matrixWorld` after transform animation; `GLTFExporter`/`OBJExporter` export of the current marching-cubes mesh compared to an upstream export at the same logical frame (semantic compare).
- Anti-cheat renamed-copy test as for H1.

## Success criteria

- Sweep (09.3) passes in the artifact; export/read tests pass; packaging harness passes on both browsers.

## Test plan

- Unit: none new.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/h2/full-artifact.mjs` on both browsers: packaging harness over the material/control sweep (09.3) in the artifact; post-update observation tests (`geometry.attributes.position.array` values, `matrixWorld`, `GLTFExporter`/`OBJExporter` output compared semantically to an upstream export at the same logical frame); renamed-copy anti-cheat diff.
- Logging: harness events per step; export comparison summary `{format, nodes, attributes, max_delta}`; archived under `evidence/11.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: exported files from both sides and the semantic diff.

## Considerations

- If a legacy shader variant fails translation, this bead is blocked (new-backend coverage gap), not narrowed.
acceptance_criteria: f3d build on the unmodified H2 source produces a standalone artifact where the addon kernel is recognized by source fingerprint and lowered, all material/control branches render through the new backend, and reading geometry/transform state or exporting the scene after an accelerated update returns current values.

title: H1/H2 equivalence validation: visual, state, control and lifecycle profiles
description:
## Full scope

H1/H2 equivalence validation: visual, state, control and lifecycle profiles at logical checkpoints with preregistered tolerances; event/state trace comparison; upstream unit-test lane green for the modules H1/H2 reach

## Summary

"Every scored application also passes image/state/interaction checks before timing results count; a green test suite alone does not establish full functionality" (§1.3).

## Background (plan §14.5, §14.6, §16.6 "Equivalence")

Compare frames and state observations at corresponding logical times; specify required causal order rather than identical wall-clock arrival; diagnostic counters may differ; excluded diagnostic pixels are narrowly identified before testing.

## Technical approach

- Run the harness-scripted sequences (03.1) on reference and candidate with identical seeds; compare at checkpoints using 03.6's tolerances (color-space-aware metric, edge/silhouette check, region checks, depth/normal diagnostic targets where the candidate exposes them).
- Trace diff for events (callbacks, loader completion, control changes) with causal-order rules.
