- Lifecycle: resize mid-run, dispose and recreate, navigation reload (H1) with state re-established.
- Upstream unit lane (18a.2) filtered to the modules reached by H1/H2 (from the closure records) must be green with owners recorded.

## Success criteria

- Equivalence profiles pass on Chrome and Safari on the M5 and Safari on the phone; failures block 11.4.

## Test plan

- Unit: none new (uses `f3d verify`'s comparison library tests from 18a.7).
- E2E: `f3d verify` on H1 (both settings) and H2 on Chrome-M5, Safari-M5 and Safari-iPhone with protocol v1 tolerances: checkpoint images, event/state traces with causal-order rules, lifecycle steps (resize mid-run, dispose/recreate, H1 navigation reload); the mapped upstream unit lane filtered to modules reached by H1/H2 must be green with owners recorded.
- Logging: per-checkpoint metrics and trace-diff events; per-test owner tags from the unit lane; archived under `evidence/11.3/<stratum>/`.
- Failure artifacts: reference/candidate/diff images and trace diffs (goldens are never regenerated from the candidate).

## Considerations

- Never regenerate goldens from the candidate; a mismatch is a defect until proven otherwise (AGENTS.md honesty rule 5).
acceptance_criteria: Both applications pass their full equivalence profile against the frozen reference: checkpoint images within the preregistered color-space-aware tolerances, identical event/state traces at corresponding logical times, all controls and lifecycle transitions (resize, disposal, reload) matching; the mapped upstream unit suites relevant to the reached modules pass with recorded owners; no speedup number is considered before this passes.

title: Scored paired runs on the phone and M5 strata (>=2x floor with 95% lower bounds)
description:
## Full scope

Scored paired runs on the iPhone 17 Pro Max and M5 strata: H1 WebGPU dynamic workload and H2 through the new renderer, full artifact including guards/materialization/bootstrap/bridge/compatibility bytes, frozen protocol, paired 95% lower bounds against the >=2x floor, cold/warm startup and memory, published with all reference configurations

## Summary

The first FrankenThreeD performance numbers, produced exactly the way the plan says numbers must be produced.

## Background (plan §16.2–16.6, §16.7; AGENTS.md "Performance Program", "Benchmark hardware discipline")

Measure completed logical frames per wall-clock second in the bounded pipeline; two frames in flight; completion acknowledgements on both sides; paired alternating runs with warmup; block bootstrap; log-space aggregation; report median, p95, p99, paired speedup, peak memory, upload totals; cold and warm startup measured separately; GPU timing runs on a reserved device with no other agent builds.

## Technical approach

- `f3d bench benchmarks/headline.toml --device <stratum>` (the bench subcommand lands here, wired into 10.8) runs the offscreen lane (03.2) for candidate and frozen reference (03.3) with the protocol's repeat count and order, collecting raw runs; the analysis script (03.8) computes the results.
- Ownership: 07.6's attribution counters must show zero retained submissions in scored frames.
- Startup: cold (cleared caches, fresh document) and warm; components: document acquisition, decoding, Wasm compile, shader/pipeline compile, asset prep, first correct frame, first interactive frame.
- Memory: peak from 10.2's accounting plus browser-reported where available.
- On-screen companion runs for pacing/input latency.

## Success criteria

- A results document per stratum with cell ratios, lower bounds, verdict per gate row (equivalence, 2× floor, confidence, tails, startup/memory, ownership), and the raw-run archive.

## Test plan

- Unit: bench-subcommand argument and protocol-loading tests; a dry run with reference-vs-reference data asserting ratios near 1.
- E2E: `f3d bench benchmarks/headline.toml --device <stratum>` for H1 (WebGPU dynamic) and H2 on the reserved phone and M5 (Safari and Chrome) with protocol v1 repeat counts and alternating order; ownership assertion (zero retained submissions) on every scored frame; cold/warm startup and on-screen companion runs; analysis via 03.8.
- Logging: raw per-frame JSON per run `{frame, submit_ts, ack_ts, credits}`; startup phase timings; capability records; the analysis report with per-cell verdicts; archived under `evidence/11.4/<stratum>/`.
- Failure artifacts: any invalidated run retained with its reason (device loss, validation error, rejected completion).

## Considerations

- An unfavorable valid run is not an infrastructure failure. An inconclusive interval means a new preregistered batch, not peeking.
- Never write "faster" anywhere until this bead's report exists (AGENTS.md honesty rule 1).
acceptance_criteria: Under protocol v1, paired alternating runs on reserved uncontended devices produce per-cell median ratios and 95% lower bounds for H1 (WebGPU dynamic setting) and H2 on Safari-phone, Safari-M5 and Chrome-M5; the new-backend ownership assertion holds for all scored frames; cold and warm startup, peak memory and tail metrics are reported against the frozen budgets; results are published with R0 and every eligible reference configuration.

title: Kill gate 3 decision record (first product gate)
description:
## Full scope

Kill gate 3 decision record: pass/fail against the first-product gate; on failure reopen the project decision rather than substituting an easier demo

## Summary

The point of Phase 1 is to be able to stop. This bead makes the decision explicit and durable.

## Background (plan §16.7, §20, §1.3 item 6)

"If H1 is not viable against its competent reference, do not replace it with an easier toy without explicitly reopening the project decision." "Do not launch the project as a performance replacement if these requirements fail. A foundation gate can stop development long before full compatibility is implemented." Responses from §20 on failure: stop or substantially revise the thesis; do not weaken the reference; change granularity/ownership; abandon per-method Wasm wrapping; keep affected state JavaScript-owned and report the cost.

## Technical approach

- `docs/gates/gate-3-first-product.md` with the table of results, the verdict, the date, the protocol version, and links to raw evidence.
- If PASS: note that broad compatibility implementation (Phase 2+) may proceed and that the result is not a universal claim.
- If FAIL: freeze the tree state, disclose exactly which condition failed, and hand the decision to the user (AGENTS.md "Mandatory checkpoint and stop rule").

## Success criteria

- The document exists and is referenced by the README's status section (the README must stop saying "no speedup measured" only when a real number exists, and must state the number with its interval and device).

## Test plan

- Unit: none (decision record).
- E2E: none; the decision cites 11.3 and 11.4 evidence directories by run id.
- Logging: the decision document lists, per stratum, the evidence run ids, the verdict per gate row and the protocol version; README status updated to state the measured number with interval and device or the FAIL.
- Failure artifacts: n/a.

## Considerations

- "A changed product decision or benchmark corpus requires a newly labeled plan/results version and cannot retroactively turn the old failed gate green" (§16.6).
acceptance_criteria: A short decision document records, per stratum, the equivalence status, the H1/H2 cell results with lower bounds, ownership verification, startup/memory/tail status, and an explicit PASS or FAIL against §16.7's first-product gate; on FAIL it records that the project decision is reopened and lists the plan's permitted responses (change granularity/ownership, keep affected state JS-owned, stop) without weakening the reference or replacing H1.

title: F3D-12 (early slice): Sound closed-island extraction for the H1 update loop, guards/materialization/codegen, and irreversible route analysis
description:
## What this epic delivers

The compiler's first real capability, scoped to what the first product gate needs. Plan §19 F3D-12 depends on 04 and 05; acceptance: "Guards/materialization before 11; escaped native access selected exactly before binding". The general island optimizer is the later closure epic (F3D-12b).

## Why (plan §4.3–4.9, §4.7 "The first compiler slice", §6.1, §3.5)

"A translation from `object.position.x = value` into an equally fine-grained Wasm call merely relocates overhead." The unit of specialization is a closed update island; a trace can suggest an island but cannot justify erasing a possible behavior; write barriers are source-level, not Proxies; guard failure must not run an update twice; specialization is partial evaluation with an explicit environment; synchronous work cannot acquire invisible yield points. "Those costs cannot be implemented after the first performance result."

## Children

1. Semantic IR and bounded worklist optimizer skeleton.
2. Semantic and effect analysis for the H1 update loop and the island admission contract.
3. Source-level write barriers.
4. Guards, safe deoptimization, materialization, dual emission and cost model.
5. Kernel code generation to application Wasm and static JS host glue.
6. Irreversible route/escape analysis.
7. Partial-evaluation environment rules.
8. Synchronous run-to-completion enforcement.
9. Build report and `f3d explain`/`f3d inspect`.

## Success criteria for the epic

All children closed; H1's update loop is lowered with guards and a conservative path; the report explains every barrier with a source span; `f3d-compiler` ships `CONTRACT.md`.

## No-claim boundary

Island extraction here covers recognized patterns for H1 (and H2's addon recognition). General numeric-loop lifting is explicitly later (§4.6).
acceptance_criteria: f3d-compiler admits a closed update island only when it can answer who mutates each value (including aliases), who reads intermediate state and when, which operations are pure, which numeric semantics are required and what invalidates the specialization; it instruments provably covered writes at build time without Proxies, emits both the optimized kernel and its conservative production path with guards that never cause double execution, materializes public state at declared boundaries, enforces the synchronous run-to-completion rule, selects exact routes for escaped native access before any binding, and produces the build report.

title: Semantic IR and bounded worklist optimizer skeleton in f3d-compiler
description:
## Full scope

Semantic IR in f3d-compiler: object identity, ownership, numeric types, update dependencies, effects, observations and source locations as typed IDs into owned arrays; bounded worklist optimizer skeleton; typed reader for the ingested module graph

## Summary

The compiler's data model, kept deliberately small.

## Background (plan §6.1, §4.1, §1.4)

"Three representations are enough... Semantic IR records object identity, ownership, numeric types, update dependencies, effects, observations, and source locations... The representations should use typed IDs into owned arrays. Avoid heap-allocated trait-object graphs in the hot path. A simple worklist optimizer with a bounded set of transformations is preferable to a general theorem prover or unrestricted equality-saturation engine." First-class objects: "application modules, semantic scene state, update kernels, render/compute passes, resources, and compiled schedules."

## Technical approach

- `f3d-compiler::ir`: arenas for `Module`, `Function`, `Stmt/Expr` (a restricted expression language for admitted numeric code plus opaque nodes for everything else), `ObjectShape` (recognized Three.js classes with known property layouts from the manifest), `Value` (numeric type lattice: JS number, int32-coerced, f32-stored; unknown), `Effect` (write to property/array/callback/host), `Observation` (read at a boundary), `Span`.
- Reader for the 04.1 bundle with schema version checks.
- Worklist: ordered pass list (recognition → alias analysis → effect analysis → island admission → guard synthesis → codegen prep) with per-pass change flags and a fixpoint cap; deterministic ordering for reproducible builds.

## Success criteria

- Round-trip test: bundle → IR → summary dump is deterministic; unit tests for arena/span handling; the optimizer reaches fixpoint on H1/H2 within the cap.
- `f3d-compiler/CONTRACT.md` is written before any other crate depends on `f3d-compiler` (AGENTS.md "Documentation and Contracts"): purpose and position in the dependency direction, public types and semantics, invariants, implementation ownership route, error model, determinism and numeric-fidelity class, cancellation behavior, unsafe boundary if any, feature flags, conformance tests, and no-claim boundaries.

## Test plan

- Unit: arena/span handling tests; bundle-reader round trip with schema-version mismatch rejected; worklist fixpoint tests (deterministic pass order; iteration cap reached on a pathological fixture reports rather than loops); fuzz target for the bundle reader (05.3 lane).
- E2E: `f3d inspect` over H1/H2 produces deterministic IR summaries (snapshot tests).
- Logging: pass-by-pass change counts `{pass, iteration, changed}` in verbose mode; archived under `evidence/12a.1/`.
- Failure artifacts: the IR dump at the failing pass.

## Considerations

- Keep the expression language restricted; unknown constructs are opaque and force JS ownership, never approximated.
acceptance_criteria: f3d-compiler defines the semantic IR with typed handles for modules, functions, objects, properties, values, effects and observations, each carrying source spans; the module-graph bundle from the ingestion adapter is read into it; a worklist optimizer runs a bounded, ordered set of passes to a fixpoint with an iteration cap; there are no heap-allocated trait-object graphs in the hot path.

title: Semantic/effect analysis for the H1 update loop and the island admission contract
description:
## Full scope

Semantic and effect analysis for the H1 update loop and the island admission contract: who mutates each value including aliases, who reads intermediate state and when, pure vs effectful operations, required numeric semantics, invalidation conditions; domain contract of ordinary guarded data properties, admitted number/array types, known call targets and covered observations; prototype changes, replaced methods, reflection, unknown callbacks, eval and escaped aliases force JavaScript ownership

## Summary

The five questions of §4.3, answered by analysis for the first real workload.

## Background (plan §4.3, §4.8, §4.4 last paragraphs, §5.3)

Admission questions: (1) Who can mutate each value, including aliases? (2) Who can read intermediate state, and when? (3) Which operations are pure numeric work, and which have effects? (4) Which numeric semantics are required? (5) What invalidates the specialization?
"Pure islands need a concrete domain contract: ordinary guarded data properties, admitted number/array types, known call targets, and covered observations. A guard must not invoke a getter or Proxy trap an extra time. Prototype changes, replaced methods, reflection, unknown callbacks, `eval`, and escaped aliases may force JavaScript ownership."
"Unknown or escaped mutations select a conservative ownership mode. In particular, arbitrary writes through a retained typed-array alias cannot generally be discovered by instrumenting only the original variable."

## Technical approach

- Recognition of Three.js shapes from the manifest (Object3D/Mesh/Material/BufferAttribute property layouts) and of the pinned upstream method semantics for calls the island uses (`Object3D.rotation.x +=`, `position.set`, `Matrix4.compose` reached via `updateMatrixWorld`).
- Alias analysis over the module graph: track references to island objects (array elements, closures, event handlers, Inspector registration); an escape to unknown code marks the object's mutable regions as JS-owned unless covered by write barriers (12a.3).
- Effect classification per statement: pure numeric; property write covered; property write uncovered (escape); callback invocation (ordered barrier); host call.
- Numeric semantics: mark operations needing JS lowering (06.1's `jsnum`), f32 storage boundaries (attribute arrays), and transcendental uses.
- Invalidation set: shape changes (prototype/method replacement detected by guards), material identity changes, object array membership changes, callback identity changes.
- Output: `IslandCandidate` records + refusal diagnostics with spans.

## Success criteria

- H1's loop admits with the expected coverage; adversarial variants refuse with the correct reasons; the analysis of H2 recognizes the addon call site as a known-kernel island (09.1) and its material selector as JS-owned control flow.

## Test plan

- Unit: analysis fixtures for H1's loop shape (admits with expected coverage) and adversarial variants (captured alias to `position`, replaced `updateMatrixWorld`, Proxy-wrapped object, `eval`, reflective access) that must refuse with the correct reason; H2 fixture recognizes the addon call site as a known-kernel island and the material selector as JS-owned control flow.
- E2E: `f3d inspect` on the ingested H1 (from 04.7) emits the island candidate report; snapshot-tested.
- Logging: per-object ownership decision table `{object, region, mode, reason, span}` in verbose builds; refusals at `warn` with spans; archived under `evidence/12a.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: the analysis report for the failing fixture.

## Considerations

- "Observing a property stay constant for 1,000 frames is not proof that it is constant" (§4.3): no trace-based admission.
acceptance_criteria: For H1's animation loop (per-object rotation/position updates from time and per-object parameters over the object array, plus the render call), the analysis produces an island candidate with the five admission answers recorded, a list of covered writes/reads, the observation boundaries (render, callbacks, Inspector reads), and refusals with spans for any construct outside the domain contract; the same analysis on adversarial variants (an alias to an object's position captured elsewhere, a replaced updateMatrixWorld, a Proxy) refuses admission.

title: Source-level write barriers (no Proxies) with conservative ownership for escapes
description:
## Full scope

Source-level write barriers: instrument provably covered writes at build time, coalesce field changes into frame or observation-boundary batches, handle aliases, compound assignment, evaluation order, setters, method overrides and exceptions; no universal JavaScript Proxies; uncovered/escaped mutations select conservative ownership with disclosed cost

## Summary

Change detection that does not change behavior.

## Background (plan §4.4)

"Instrument provably covered writes at build time. Coalesce the resulting field changes into a frame or observation-boundary batch. Account for aliases, compound assignments, evaluation order, setters, method overrides, and exceptions. Do not wrap the entire application in JavaScript Proxies... Respect Three.js's explicit upload-version contract where it applies; where additional synchronization is needed, pay for a scan/copy or retain the state in JavaScript and disclose the cost. The compiler must not claim work proportional only to the number of changed fields unless its mutation coverage actually supports that claim."

## Technical approach

- Rewrite pass (in the JS emission side of the compiler, using the pinned AST toolchain for printing): for each covered write site, emit the original write plus a barrier call recording (object handle, field id) into a typed dirty batch (bitset in Wasm memory or a JS typed array flushed at the boundary); preserve evaluation order by binding the RHS to a temporary before the barrier when the RHS could throw.
- Setters/`_onChange`: Three.js `Euler`/`Quaternion` use change callbacks; barriers integrate with those semantics (06.4) rather than duplicating them.
- Exceptions: a throw after several writes leaves the batch consistent with what upstream would have observed (no rollback, no missing dirty bits).
- Uncovered regions: the region is JS-owned (snapshot at boundary via a bounded scan/copy) with the scanned byte count in the report.
- Measurement: barrier cost per write and batch flush cost, reported via 07.7.

## Success criteria

- H1 with barriers produces identical traces to unmodified H1; dirty batches exactly match the set of written fields under property tests including compound assignments and exceptions; escaped-alias fixture routes to scan/copy with the cost reported.

## Test plan

- Unit: AST-level rewrite tests per construct (simple write, compound assignment, setter, overridden method, throwing RHS, alias write); property tests on generated write sequences asserting the dirty batch equals the set of written fields; escaped-alias fixture routes to scan/copy with the byte count in the report.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/compiler/barriers.mjs`: H1 with barriers produces identical traces to unmodified H1 on both browsers; barrier overhead measured via 07.7 counters.
- Logging: barrier counts and batch sizes per frame (debug) and the scan/copy byte counts per region; archived under `evidence/12a.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: the rewritten source excerpt and the batch diff.

## Considerations

- Never introduce accessors where descriptors/enumeration are observable (§4.8).
acceptance_criteria: The compiler rewrites covered write sites in the application's own source (static output, no Proxies) to record field changes into a batch consumed at the next observation boundary; aliases, compound assignments, evaluation order, setters, overrides and exceptions are handled with tests; writes the analysis cannot cover route the region to JavaScript ownership or a scan/copy path whose byte cost appears in the report; the barrier overhead is measured.

title: Guards, safe deoptimization, materialization, dual emission and cost model
description:
## Full scope

Guards, safe deoptimization and materialization: guards validate shape/material/callback assumptions before pure kernels run; effectful blocks stay ordered barriers; guard failure never double-executes an update; declared materialization boundaries preserve identity; both the optimized kernel and its conservative production path are emitted; the cost model includes guard scans and facade traffic and keeps small or frequently observed islands in JavaScript

## Summary

Specialization that is safe to be wrong about.

## Background (plan §4.5, §4.8, §14.8; AGENTS.md counterexample "Guard failure without double-execution")

"A specialized island may depend on a material configuration, object shape, or callback identity. A guard validates these assumptions before the affected work executes. On guard failure, invalidate the relevant plan and use the compatibility execution path until a new specialization is ready. Guard failure must not cause the application to run an update twice... pure kernels are guarded before execution, and effectful blocks remain ordered barriers unless a stronger transformation is justified." "Emit both the optimized kernel and its production conservative path. Define guard failure, materialization, and re-entry before emitting optimized code. The cost model includes guard scans and facade traffic, not just the inner Rust loop. Small or frequently observed islands should remain JavaScript when crossing/packing costs dominate." "Guards/materialization are part of the measured optimized path, not disabled in benchmark mode."

## Technical approach

- Guard synthesis from 12a.2's invalidation set: cheap checks (prototype identity, method identity, material identity/keys, array length/identity, callback identity) executed before the kernel; guard must not invoke getters/Proxy traps.
- Deopt protocol: on failure, mark the plan segment invalid, execute the conservative path (the original JS statements, still with barriers) for this operation, schedule re-specialization off the hot path (region policy 02.5).
- Materialization: per island, the boundary set (render, callbacks, explicit reads discovered by analysis, exporter entry) where packed state is published to public objects (06.4 mechanism).
- Cost model: constants measured by micro-runs in 03.5/05.6 (crossing cost, bytes/µs packing); an island is admitted only if estimated savings exceed guard + facade cost with margin; decision recorded in the report.
- Tests: guard failure after a side-effecting statement in the same source operation → no double effect; deopt after replacing a method at runtime; an intentionally tiny island stays JS.

## Success criteria

- Counterexample and deopt tests pass; H1's island admitted with its cost line; a synthetic small-island fixture refused by cost.

## Test plan

- Unit: guard synthesis tests from invalidation sets; guard-failure-without-double-execution counterexample (side effect before the failing guard runs exactly once); deopt-after-method-replacement test; cost-model tests with measured constants (a tiny island is refused; H1's island admitted with its cost line); a test that guards never invoke getters/Proxy traps.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/compiler/guards.mjs` on both browsers: runtime method replacement at a random frame falls back correctly with trace equality; mutation check disabling the guard demonstrates the failure it prevents.
- Logging: guard outcomes per frame (bounded) `{island, guards_checked, failures, deopts}`; re-specialization events off the hot path; archived under `evidence/12a.4/`.
- Failure artifacts: the trace around the guard failure and the cost-model inputs.

## Considerations

- Re-specialization is off the hot path; it never blocks a synchronous operation (§4.9).
acceptance_criteria: Every admitted island has a guard set, a materialization plan and a conservative path; a guard failure mid-frame falls back to the conservative path for that operation without re-running already-performed side effects (counterexample test); the cost model's inputs (guard scan cost, packing/unpacking bytes, crossing counts) are measured constants per device and a small island is demonstrably kept in JS; deoptimization after an assumption change is tested.

title: Kernel code generation to application Wasm plus static JS host glue
description:
## Full scope

Kernel code generation: admitted islands to generated Rust kernels compiled into the application-specific Wasm with the pinned nightly; static JavaScript host glue (no eval/new Function); input packing and output materialization; H1 update kernel producing packed AffineRows uploads

## Summary

From island to executable, end to end.

## Background (plan §4.1, §4.6 row 1, §6.4, §17.2)

"Generated Rust kernels are compiled into an application-specific Wasm module with the pinned nightly toolchain." "Many object transforms updated from time and numeric parameters → Bulk CPU Wasm kernel and packed transform upload." "Generate ordinary static JavaScript source: no production `eval` or `new Function` requirement." "Application-specific generated kernels are also reported per artifact; generators must not be used to disguise a giant checked-in engine."

## Technical approach

- Rust codegen templates for the restricted expression language: loops over packed SoA arrays (06.2), `jsnum` calls where required, f32 conversions at the same boundaries as the source; kernel signature takes handles/ranges, returns nothing; results land in packed state that 06.4 materializes and 08.1 uploads.
- Build integration: a generated `app-kernels` crate compiled by the CLI with the pinned toolchain into the single application Wasm (Asupersync + f3d runtime + kernels); build cache keys (10.6).
- JS glue emission: static module with the barrier batch flush, kernel invocation at the source's synchronous call site (the animation loop statement is replaced by `kernel_update_h1(t, ...)` plus the conservative fallback under the guard), and materialization calls.
- Generated-code report: line counts and bytes per artifact.

## Success criteria

- H1 builds with its kernel; trace equality vs unmodified H1; uploads are packed `AffineRows` ranges; the generated Rust is readable and free of unsafe.

## Test plan

- Unit: golden tests for generated Rust and JS on fixtures (no `unsafe`, no `eval`/`new Function`); build-integration test compiling the generated crate with the pinned toolchain into the single application Wasm; input packing/output materialization round-trip tests.
- E2E: H1 builds with its kernel; `tests/e2e/compiler/kernel-h1.mjs` asserts trace equality vs unmodified H1 and that uploads are packed AffineRows ranges (counters) on both browsers.
- Logging: codegen summary in the build report `{islands, generated_rust_lines, generated_js_lines, wasm_bytes}`; archived under `evidence/12a.5/`.
- Failure artifacts: the generated sources and the compiler diagnostics.

## Considerations

- The kernel runs to completion synchronously (12a.8); no chunk yields.
acceptance_criteria: The compiler emits Rust source for admitted islands (H1's per-object update loop over packed arrays using f3d-math with JS numeric lowering), compiles it with f3d-core/f3d-math/f3d-scene into one application Wasm linked with the Asupersync runtime, and emits static JS glue that packs inputs at the boundary, invokes the kernel synchronously, and materializes outputs; the generated code is reported per artifact and never disguises a checked-in engine.

title: Irreversible route and escape analysis feeding the construction hook
description:
## Full scope

Irreversible route and escape analysis: detect renderer/canvas/native state escaping to opaque code that may call GL-specific or native-backend methods, required native contracts (sync readback, getContext, XR fallback), and select the exact component before any binding; report decisions with source spans

## Summary

The compile-time half of "the backend choice is irreversible".

## Background (plan §5.6, §6.9, §20 "Late backend choice breaks canvas identity")

"The source/runtime and dependency analysis determines the safe selection before an irreversible canvas/device/native-handle binding. Unknown future native use through escaped references requires conservative exact selection." "If a renderer or its canvas/native state can escape to opaque code that may call GL-specific or native-backend methods, preserve the corresponding exact component from construction. If the source closes those observations, its non-native work can use the new backend without carrying legacy decisions in the hot loop."

## Technical approach

- Escape analysis on the IR: track the renderer object, its `domElement`/canvas, `getContext()` results, `renderer.state`/`properties` accessors, `xr` manager; any flow into unknown callee, global, event handler, or retained addon whose fingerprint indicates native use → escape.
- Native contract detection: calls to `readRenderTargetPixels` (sync), `getContext`, `resetState`, `forceContextLoss`, `GLBufferAttribute` construction, `WebGLXRFallback`, explicit `WebGLRenderer` construction, `forceWebGL`-style options.
- Output: `RouteDecision { site, route, reasons, spans }` consumed by 04.4; report section.

## Success criteria

- Fixtures pass (exact for escape/native contracts, new-backend for closed cases); H1's two branches classified correctly; H2 (WebGLRenderer as authored with no native observations) classified as new-backend-eligible for the accelerated route with the exact component retained for its functional GL lane only if the source contract requires it (record the reasoning).

## Test plan

- Unit: escape-analysis fixtures (renderer passed to an unknown plugin → exact; `readRenderTargetPixels` sync use → exact; `getContext` → exact; `WebGLXRFallback` → exact; closed observations → new-backend-eligible); decision snapshot for the corpus (H1 both branches; H2 reasoning recorded).
- E2E: 04.4's routing hook consumes the decisions for H1/H2 in the routed builds; the report shows spans and reasons.
- Logging: decision table `{site, span, route, reasons}`; archived under `evidence/12a.6/`.
- Failure artifacts: the flow trace that produced a wrong classification.

## Considerations

- "Do not assume arbitrary subclasses can be reproduced by a name-based shim" (§5.6): unknown `Renderer`/`Backend` subclasses are exact by default.
acceptance_criteria: The analysis classifies every renderer construction site as new-backend-eligible or exact-required using conservative escape analysis and native-contract detection; the routing hook consumes the classification before binding; H1's WebGL branch and a fixture passing the renderer to an unknown plugin both select exact; a fixture with closed observations selects the new backend; each decision carries spans and reasons in the report.

title: Partial-evaluation environment rules (no baking of unbound runtime state)
description:
## Full scope

Partial-evaluation environment rules: offline evaluation only for inputs proven independent of unbound runtime state; DOM, viewport, adapter, query string, locale, clock, random values and network responses are not constants; preserve random-source consumption and observable construction/ID ordering; runtime-created objects and unobserved branches remain executable

## Summary

Specialization is partial evaluation with an explicit environment, not snapshotting.

## Background (plan §4.8, §3.1)

"Offline evaluation is allowed only for inputs proven independent of unbound runtime state. A captured DOM, viewport, adapter, query string, locale, clock, random value, or successful network response is not automatically an application constant. Preserve random-source consumption and observable construction/ID ordering when baking work would otherwise advance them differently. Runtime-created objects and unobserved branches remain executable; a capture is not a complete application specification."

## Technical approach

- Environment model in the IR: a set of unbound sources with taint propagation; constant folding stops at tainted values.
- ID/random preservation: any baked construction must reproduce the same `Object3D.id`/`Material.id` sequence and `Math.random` consumption count as the runtime path (either do not bake constructions, or emit an explicit "advance counters" prologue proven equivalent).
- Branch executability: dead-code elimination uses static reachability only; capture data is advisory (for variant precompilation priority), never for removal.

## Success criteria

- Fixtures pass; H1's `count`/`dynamic` URL-parameter branches remain executable in the artifact; ID sequences match upstream in trace tests.

## Test plan

- Unit: taint-lattice tests (each unbound source stops folding); ID/random preservation tests (baked construction reproduces the same `Object3D.id` sequence and `Math.random` consumption count as runtime); a captured-trace fixture proving no branch is eliminated from capture data.
- E2E: H1's URL-parameter branches remain executable in the artifact (packaging harness); ID-sequence equality vs upstream in the browser.
- Logging: list of folded constants with proof sources and the counter-advance prologue if emitted; archived under `evidence/12a.7/`.
- Failure artifacts: the folding decision with its taint path.

## Considerations

- Interacts with 10.4 (capture is sandboxed and untrusted).
acceptance_criteria: The compiler's constant-folding/baking passes consult an explicit environment model that marks the listed sources as unbound; a fixture that reads window.innerWidth or Math.random at module scope is not baked; object ID ordering (Object3D.id counters) and random consumption are preserved relative to upstream; a captured trace can never mark a branch as dead.

title: Synchronous run-to-completion enforcement and the sync-yield counterexample
description:
## Full scope

Synchronous run-to-completion enforcement: admitted synchronous kernels never acquire host yield points; chunking only for source-asynchronous work, isolated worker jobs, or proven interleaving equivalence; exceptions and partial effects preserved; synchronous-yield interleaving counterexample; honest cancellation-latency bound reporting

## Summary

A cooperative runtime does not get to change the browser's run-to-completion semantics.

## Background (plan §4.9, §11.3, §6.3; AGENTS.md "Synchronous work cannot acquire invisible yield points"; counterexample "Synchronous-yield interleaving")

"Doing so can expose half-updated state, alter Promise ordering, or deliver user input inside a computation that previously ran to completion... Preserve source exceptions and partial effects: an effectful loop that throws after several mutations cannot be replaced by an all-or-nothing bulk commit unless those intermediate effects are unobservable. Partial numeric work may use scratch output and commit only where that is actually equivalent."

## Technical approach

- Type-level enforcement: kernels are plain synchronous functions; the runtime's frame path has no async entry; a lint in the compiler rejects any emitted `await`/timer inside a synchronous island; chunked execution is available only through region tasks for source-async work (02.5).
- Exceptions: the kernel's numeric work writes scratch output and commits per element in source order when effects are observable, or bulk-commits only when the analysis proves intermediate effects unobservable; on a thrown exception (from a guarded callback or a coerced non-numeric operand), state matches upstream's partial state.
- Counterexample test: a source loop with a microtask scheduled mid-way (`queueMicrotask`) and a synchronous read after the loop; a deliberately chunked implementation shows the divergence; the candidate matches upstream.
- Cancellation bound: for kernels exceeding a threshold, the report states that cancellation cannot be observed before the kernel returns.

## Success criteria

- Counterexample and exception-partial-effect tests pass; lint rejects a synthetic yielding kernel.

## Test plan

- Unit: compiler lint rejecting a synthetic yielding kernel; exception-partial-effect tests (throw after N mutations leaves exactly upstream's partial state); scratch-commit equivalence tests.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/compiler/sync-yield.mjs` on both browsers: a source loop with a microtask scheduled mid-way and a synchronous read after it; the deliberately chunked implementation diverges, the candidate matches upstream; kernel-duration histogram collected.
- Logging: kernel duration `metric` events feeding the cancellation-bound statement in the report; the interleaving trace on failure; archived under `evidence/12a.8/`.
- Failure artifacts: the trace diff showing the exposed intermediate state.

## Considerations

- "Unknown/non-numeric operands stay on the JavaScript path rather than introducing a Rust panic or an unintended coercion" (§5.4).
acceptance_criteria: The compiler and runtime cannot insert an await or host yield inside an originally synchronous source operation; an effectful loop that throws after several mutations keeps its partial effects on the candidate exactly as upstream; a counterexample test proves that splitting the update across turns would expose half-updated state or alter Promise ordering and that the candidate does not; the report states the cancellation-latency bound for long synchronous kernels.

title: Build report (text and stable JSON), f3d explain and f3d inspect
description:
## Full scope

Build report (human text and stable JSON) and f3d explain/inspect: Three.js version and asset/module hashes; specialized/general/retained/exact ownership; functional gaps vs host limitations vs optimization-only barriers with no status conversion; structural cost estimates distinct from measured timings; precise source spans and reasons for barriers; unlock suggestions; device profile and optional capability variants

## Summary

The report that makes the compiler useful to humans and coding agents alike.

## Background (plan §3.5, §5.7, §13.5, §16.9)

"Every build should explain, in human-readable text and stable JSON: the selected Three.js version and asset/module hashes; which work was specialized, executed by the general backend, retained in JS, or kept on an exact backend; distinct functional gaps, host/source limitations, and optimization-only barriers, with no conversion of one status into another; estimated structural costs, clearly distinguished from measured timings; precise source spans and reasons for specialization barriers; changes needed to unlock a fast path without weakening behavior; the selected device profile and optional capability variants. For example, a report might explain that a typed array escapes to an unknown plugin, so safe change detection requires a conservative copy; it should identify that escape and the copied byte count. It must not claim a measured improvement before a benchmark runs."

## Technical approach

- Report schema (versioned JSON, serde in `f3d-compiler`): header (pin, hashes), ownership table (per module/object region/renderer), islands (admitted with guards and cost estimates; refused with spans/reasons/unlock hints), routes (12a.6), variants (08.3), assets (10.1), retained components and bytes (04.3/13.5), estimates section, measurements section (empty until `f3d bench` attaches results), capability profile.
- Text renderer with stable ordering; `f3d inspect` runs analysis without codegen.
- Source maps for generated kernels/JS so spans point to original application lines (§16.9).

## Success criteria

- H1/H2 reports snapshot-tested; the escape example above is reproduced by a fixture; schema validated.

## Test plan

- Unit: report schema validation; snapshot tests for H1/H2 reports (text and JSON); the plan's escape example reproduced by a fixture (typed array escapes to an unknown plugin → conservative copy with byte count and span); source-map resolution tests for generated kernel/JS spans.
- E2E: `f3d explain` and `f3d inspect` CLI tests over the corpus artifacts; the measurements section is empty until a bench result is attached (asserted).
- Logging: none beyond the report; schema-version events in verbose mode.
- Failure artifacts: the report diff on snapshot changes.

## Considerations

- "Distinguish structural cost estimates from measured timings everywhere they appear" (AGENTS.md honesty rule 8).
acceptance_criteria: Every build emits demo.f3d-report.json plus text with the enumerated sections; statuses are never converted between categories; estimates are labeled as estimates; every barrier has a span and a reason; f3d explain renders it and f3d inspect produces the analysis-only form for a source without building; no measured-improvement claim appears unless a bench result is attached.

title: F3D-12 (closure): Generalize island extraction, aliases/effects/guards, ownership/materialization, dirty propagation and dynamic topology without losing public functionality
description:
## What this epic delivers

Phase 2's compiler generalization. Plan §18 Phase 2: "Generalize aliases/effects/guards, ownership/materialization, dirty propagation, dynamic topology, animation and procedural kernels... Exit: held-out applications and dynamic input sequences work without F3D-specific valid-input refusals. Tests prove both successful specialization and conservative exact/general execution."

## Why (plan §4.6 last sentence, §14.8, §18 Phase 2, §22)

"General numeric-loop lifting follows these recognized paths; it must not become a prerequisite for the first useful result." Now that the first result exists, generalization must not lose any public functionality: "Preserve the complete scalar/public API via retained modules where that is best; shared state must remain correct for controls, raycasts, cloning, serialization and exporters immediately after optimized updates."

## Children

1. General alias/effect analysis and the §4.6 pattern lowerings.
2. Ownership/materialization generalization for shared state.
3. Dynamic topology and structural plan rebuilds.
4. Held-out corpus and unseen input sequences with deoptimization tests.
5. Per-pass legality statements, conservative references, counterexamples and ablations.

## Success criteria for the epic

All children closed; the generalization gate (G4) can be evaluated with these results.

## No-claim boundary

No "general JavaScript compilation" (optional research tier). Unrecognized code stays JavaScript-owned and executable.
acceptance_criteria: The compiler admits islands for the §4.6 pattern table beyond H1/H2 (repeated geometry/material, stable material/lighting, known AnimationMixer paths, procedural addons, TSL graphs, retained DOM controls) under generalized alias/effect analysis; shared state stays correct for controls, raycasts, cloning, serialization and exporters immediately after optimized updates; dynamic insertion/removal/reparenting/layout changes rebuild only affected plans; held-out applications and unseen input sequences work with no F3D-specific valid-input refusals; each optimizer pass has a legality statement, conservative reference, counterexamples and an ablation.

title: General alias/effect analysis and the section 4.6 pattern lowerings
description:
## Full scope

General alias/effect analysis and the §4.6 pattern lowerings: repeated geometry/material with differing transforms or colors to instance streams; stable material/lighting combinations to prebuilt variants and bindings; known AnimationMixer/track paths to batched interpolation preserving public events; known procedural addons to safe kernels; TSL graphs with known node semantics to WGSL and persistent plans; DOM controls and unusual effectful callbacks retained with boundary synchronization

## Summary

Extend the compiler from "H1's loop" to the plan's first-compilation-target table.

## Background (plan §4.6, §4.3, §4.4, §12.3)

| Pattern | Initial lowering |
|---|---|
| Many object transforms updated from time and numeric parameters | Bulk CPU Wasm kernel and packed transform upload |
| Repeated geometry/material with differing transforms or colors | Instance stream or equivalent grouped draw plan |
| Stable material/lighting combinations | Prebuilt shader variants and bindings |
| Known AnimationMixer/track paths | Batched interpolation and pose propagation, preserving public events |
| Known procedural geometry addon | Safe Rust kernel behind the same API contract |
| TSL graph with known node semantics | WGSL generation and persistent resource/pass plan |
| DOM controls and unusual effectful callbacks | Retain JavaScript and synchronize at explicit boundaries |

## Technical approach

- Generalize alias analysis to interprocedural flows within the application module graph (bounded context sensitivity), with escape classes: module-local, addon-internal (fingerprinted), unknown.
- Pattern recognizers keyed on manifest shapes and pinned addon fingerprints; admission contracts per pattern (for example AnimationMixer: mixer/actions/clips not subclassed, no custom `PropertyBinding` overrides, event listeners preserved as ordered effects).
- Lowerings reuse F3D-08 (instances/variants), F3D-13 (animation kernels), F3D-09-style kernels, F3D-07.5/F3D-16 (TSL).
- Held-out discipline: recognizers are semantic (shape + fingerprint), never example-path based.

## Success criteria

- H3 (animation multiple) and H5 (instancing dynamic) admit their expected islands; H4/H6 admit the stable-material and grouping patterns; synthetic negative fixtures refuse; reports explain.

## Test plan

- Unit: recognizer tests per §4.6 pattern on synthetic applications (repeated geometry/material; stable material/lighting; AnimationMixer paths with and without subclassing; procedural addon by fingerprint; TSL graph; DOM controls) asserting admission or refusal with reasons; interprocedural alias fixtures (module-local, addon-internal, unknown escape).
- E2E: trace-equivalence runs on H3–H6 and held-out apps via `f3d verify` in the forced-new-backend lane on both browsers; the build reports list admitted islands per pattern.
- Logging: per-pattern admission counts and refusal reasons with spans; archived under `evidence/12b.1/`.
- Failure artifacts: the analysis report for the wrongly admitted/refused fixture.

## Considerations

- Effectful callbacks remain ordered barriers unless a stronger transformation is justified (§4.5).
acceptance_criteria: Each pattern in the §4.6 table has a recognizer, an admission contract and a lowering with tests on synthetic applications and on H3–H6; unrecognized code remains JS-owned and executable; every refusal is reported with a span and an unlock hint.

title: Ownership/materialization generalization for shared state after optimized updates
description:
## Full scope

Ownership and materialization generalization: shared state stays correct for controls, raycasts, cloning, serialization and exporters immediately after optimized updates; mirrored-epoch regions with explicit publication; escaped typed-array aliases handled by scan/copy with disclosed cost

## Summary

Extend 06.4's guarantees from H1/H2's specific reads to every public read path the generalized islands can affect.

## Background (plan §5.3, §5.10, §18 Phase 2)

"Shared state must remain correct for controls, raycasts, cloning, serialization and exporters immediately after optimized updates."

## Technical approach

- Enumerate read paths per admitted pattern from the manifest (which public methods read which fields); materialization boundaries extended accordingly; where a read is discovered only at runtime (reflection), the guard on the region falls back to JS ownership.
- Mirrored-epoch regions for animation state (mixer time/weights) and instance data, with `publish()` at the source boundaries.
- Tests: for each corpus app, inject a read of each kind at random logical frames and compare to upstream.

## Success criteria

- All injected reads match; no region has two writers (05.5 invariant check enabled in tests).

## Test plan

- Unit: read-path enumeration tests from the manifest (which public methods read which fields); mirrored-epoch publication tests; property tests over read-injection schedules with the single-writer invariant check enabled.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/compiler/read-paths.mjs` on H3–H6 and held-out apps: OrbitControls reads, `Raycaster` over accelerated meshes, `clone()`, `toJSON()`, `GLTFExporter` injected at random logical frames and compared to upstream on both browsers.
- Logging: materialization and publication events per region `{region, mode, epoch, trigger}`; mismatch events with property path and values; archived under `evidence/12b.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: serialized object graphs from both sides.

## Considerations

- Do not defer an observable animation update to a convenient frame commit (§5.10).
acceptance_criteria: Any public read path (OrbitControls reading camera state, Raycaster over accelerated meshes, object.clone(), toJSON(), GLTFExporter) observes current values immediately after an optimized update, across all admitted patterns; mirrored regions publish at explicit epochs; escaped-alias regions are JS-owned with the scan bytes in the report; tests cover each read path on H3–H6 and held-out apps.

title: Dynamic topology and structural plan rebuilds
description:
## Full scope

Dynamic topology and structural plan rebuilds: insertion, removal, reparenting and resource-layout changes rebuild only the affected structural plan segments (buckets, bundles, dependency closures); dirty propagation generalized to arbitrary scene edits at runtime

## Summary

The compiled plan must survive the application changing its own structure.

## Background (plan §6.2 last paragraph, §18 Phase 2)

"Dynamic insertion, removal, reparenting, and resource-layout changes rebuild only the affected structural plan."

## Technical approach

- Structural event stream (06.3) drives segment invalidation: buckets (08.1), bundles (08.4), dependency closures (06.3), material variant bindings (08.3), pass graph resources (07.2); each with a locality test.
- Rebuild cost measured and reported in the interaction-tail metrics (§16.9).

## Success criteria

- Locality counters; trace equality on edit scripts; rebuild latencies recorded.

## Test plan

- Unit: property tests over random edit sequences (add/remove/reparent, geometry/material replacement, attribute layout change, light/render-target addition) asserting locality counters (only affected segments rebuilt) and correctness against a Node oracle.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/compiler/topology.mjs` on H1/H3/H5 and held-out apps with scripted edits on both browsers; trace equality; rebuild latencies recorded for the interaction-tail report.
- Logging: structural events and rebuilt segments `{event, segments_rebuilt, ms}`; archived under `evidence/12b.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: the plan diff before/after the edit.

## Considerations

- Edits inside callbacks during render obey reentrancy rules (07.4).
acceptance_criteria: Runtime scene edits (add/remove/reparent objects, replace geometries/materials, change attribute layouts, add lights, add render targets) invalidate and rebuild only affected plan segments with counters proving locality; correctness is preserved (trace equality) on scripted edit sequences over H1/H3/H5 and held-out apps.

title: Held-out application corpus and unseen input sequences with deoptimization tests
description:
## Full scope

Held-out application corpus and unseen input sequences: a set of applications not used for tuning runs through the same compiler with no example-path selection or captured-output replay; deoptimization after assumption changes and dynamic input sequences are tested; no F3D-specific valid-input refusals

## Summary

Proof that the compiler generalizes rather than memorizes.

## Background (plan §14.8, §16.7 "Generalization gate", §18 Phase 2 exit, §20 "Full-suite success hides untested missing features")

"A held-out source corpus and unseen input/control sequences must exercise the same compiler; selecting kernels by example path or replaying captured outputs is disallowed." Phase 2 exit: "held-out applications and dynamic input sequences work without F3D-specific valid-input refusals."

## Technical approach

- Preregister the held-out list in `benchmarks/heldout-v1.toml` before generalization work uses them (record the date); include varied families (an animation example, an instancing example, a postprocessing example, a loader example, a controls-heavy example, a CSS/SVG example).
- Unseen input scripts generated from a different seed family than the tuning scripts.
- Deopt scenarios injected via the harness at random frames.

## Success criteria

- All held-out apps pass equivalence; deopt scenarios match upstream; zero refusals.

## Test plan

- Unit: none new; the held-out list file is schema-validated and its preregistration date checked.
- E2E: build and `f3d verify` every preregistered held-out application with unseen input scripts (different seed family) on both browsers; deopt scenarios injected at random frames (method replacement, buffer aliasing, material key change); zero valid-input refusals asserted from the reports.
- Logging: per-app summary `{app, islands_admitted, refusals, verify_result, deopts_triggered}`; archived under `evidence/12b.4/`.
- Failure artifacts: verify artifacts and the refusal list.

## Considerations

- Held-out performance is measured in G4/F3D-23, not here; this bead is about functionality and generalization.
acceptance_criteria: At least a preregistered set of held-out upstream examples (chosen from the pinned index outside H1–H8 and outside the tuning set) build and pass equivalence with unseen input scripts; deopt tests mutate assumptions at runtime (replace a method, alias a buffer, change a material key) and the candidate falls back correctly; any valid-input refusal is a blocking defect.

title: Per-optimizer-pass legality statements, conservative references, counterexamples, ablation toggles
description:
## Full scope

Per-optimizer-pass evidence: a legality statement, a conservative executable reference, counterexample tests and an ablation toggle for every pass (update compilation, dirty tracking, program merging, instancing, bundles, upload coalescing, pass/resource optimization)

## Summary

The plan's evidence discipline for optimizations, applied uniformly.

## Background (plan §14.8, §16.8)

"Each optimizer pass needs a small legality statement, a conservative executable reference, counterexample tests, and an ablation measurement." "Use a few strong invariants rather than a large bureaucracy: one owner per mutable epoch, no stale publication, preserved observation order, legal resource usage, and no optimization result accepted before equivalence passes."

## Technical approach

- A registry of passes with metadata (name, legality doc link, conservative-path switch, counterexample test names); the ablation harness (F3D-20.5) iterates it.
- Keep this as a small table plus conventions, not a framework.

## Success criteria

- Registry complete for all existing passes; CI-free local check that every pass has all four items.

## Test plan

- Unit: a registry-consistency test asserting every pass has a legality doc link, a conservative-path switch, at least one counterexample test name that resolves, and an ablation entry; each counterexample test fails when its pass's legality rule is bypassed (mutation runs).
- E2E: the ablation harness (20.5) iterates the registry once on a small scene to prove every switch is live.
- Logging: registry dump and mutation-run results `{pass, counterexample, detected: bool}`; archived under `evidence/12b.5/`.
- Failure artifacts: the undetected mutation's diff.

## Considerations

- "The reference is available for development comparisons; production does not double-render every frame to prove itself continuously" (§14.8).
acceptance_criteria: Each optimizer pass is documented with its legality statement in the crate docs, has a switch that routes to its conservative reference, has at least one counterexample test that fails when the legality rule is violated, and is measurable in isolation by the ablation harness.

title: F3D-13: Complete animation/math/geometry scalar behavior and bulk kernels
description:
## What this epic delivers

Closure of the CPU-side feature families and the animation gain path. Plan §19 F3D-13 depends on 06, 11 and 12 (early); acceptance: "All contracts via real owners; event/IK/retarget/query/export combinations and held-out gains".

## Why (plan §5.12 rows Math, Scene graph, Geometry, Curves, Animation; §7.7; §15.2 H3/H5)

"Complete retained contract with batched Rust kernels; synchronous state and callback/event order; not just sampled poses." "Retained reference-compatible scalar surface; safe Rust bulk kernels when proven; edge cases, coercions, mutability, return identity."

## Children

1. Animation contract and batched kernels.
2. Skeleton/skinning/morph CPU path, retargeting/IK/character utilities, dual-quaternion as opt-in.
3. Math family closure.
4. Geometry and attributes family closure.
5. Curves/shapes/modifiers/CSG closure.
6. Scene graph and core data family closure.
7. Procedural geometry kernels beyond marching cubes and the GPU-generation legality rule.
8. H3/H5 end-to-end routes and held-out measurement.

## Success criteria for the epic

All children closed; the manifest shows every record in these families with an owner and positive behavioral test reference; no `unclassified`/`unimplemented` in these families.

## No-claim boundary

Retained modules count as compositional compatibility, not Rust feature coverage (§14.3).
acceptance_criteria: Every animation, math, scene-graph, geometry/attribute and curve/shape/modifier contract in the manifest has a real production owner (retained reference-compatible scalar surface or proven Rust kernel) with edge cases, coercions, mutability and return identity tested; batched animation kernels preserve synchronous state and callback/event order; H3 and H5 have measured end-to-end routes on held-out inputs.

title: Animation contract and batched kernels (events, mixer state, synchronous observation)
description:
## Full scope

Animation contract and batched kernels: every clip/action/mixer/group/track/interpolant, property binding and mixing, blending/additive/crossfade/loop/events; batched interpolation and pose propagation preserving interpolation type, track ordering, event times, loop events, morph weights and observable mixer state; AnimationMixer.update results visible synchronously; pose caching only when time/weights/skeleton agree; invariant data shared without forcing shared poses

## Summary

Animation as ordered effects with a fast interior.

## Background (plan §5.12 "Animation and deformation", §7.7, §5.10, §4.6 row 4)

"For recognized animation paths, lower interpolation, pose propagation, and buffer packing together. Preserve interpolation type, track ordering, additive/blended behavior, event times, loop events, morph weights, and observable mixer state. Animation events remain ordered effects, not GPU-only state. Cache pose work only when source time/weights and skeleton state agree. Share invariant data across instances without forcing all instances to share a pose." "`AnimationMixer.update()`... can synchronously observe results before `renderer.render()` is called. Finish or materialize the results at those original boundaries."

## Technical approach

- Retain upstream animation classes as the public contract; the compiler recognizes the mixer update call and the bound property set (12b.1); the kernel evaluates tracks (linear/step/cubic interpolants with upstream's exact math incl. `CubicInterpolant` and quaternion slerp flavors), applies blending/additive/weights with upstream's `PropertyMixer` accumulation order, writes results to packed targets (transforms, morph weights) and materializes to public objects at `update()` return.
- Events: computed in the kernel as an ordered list and dispatched via the retained `EventDispatcher` in upstream order after the numeric pass, at the same logical point.
- Unbindable/unusual bindings (custom property paths, non-numeric targets) stay on the retained path per binding.
- Pose cache keyed on (clip, time, weights, skeleton generation).

## Success criteria

- Upstream animation unit tests pass (routed); differential traces on H3 and animation examples show identical poses, events and mixer state at every update; kernel path attribution shows batched evaluation for recognized cases.

## Test plan

- Unit: property tests over track/interpolant types (linear/step/cubic, quaternion slerp flavors), blending/additive/weights with upstream's `PropertyMixer` accumulation order, loop modes and event times against a Node oracle; pose-cache key tests; unusual-binding fixtures staying on the retained path.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/animation/mixer.mjs` on H3 and animation examples on both browsers: identical poses, events (`loop`, `finished`) and mixer state at every `AnimationMixer.update` boundary; mapped upstream animation unit tests green; kernel attribution shows batched evaluation for recognized cases.
- Logging: per-update `metric` events `{tracks_evaluated, events_emitted, batched: bool}`; mismatch events with track name, time and both values; archived under `evidence/13.1/`.
- Failure artifacts: pose dumps and event traces from both sides.

## Considerations

- Retargeting/IK are 13.2; export after animation is 19.4.
acceptance_criteria: All animation-family manifest records have owners: retained upstream classes for the public contract, with recognized mixer/track paths lowered to batched Rust kernels whose outputs and event sequences equal upstream at every AnimationMixer.update boundary; property bindings to arbitrary targets remain correct; events ('loop', 'finished') fire in upstream order and time; H3's mixers are lowered.

title: Skeleton/skinning/morph CPU path, retargeting/IK utilities, dual-quaternion as opt-in
description:
## Full scope

Skeleton, skinning and morph CPU path plus retargeting/IK/character utilities: matrix-based skinning by default, bone matrices/bind matrices/skeleton textures materialized as upstream, morph target influences and relative morphs, SkeletonUtils retargeting, CCDIKSolver and related helpers retained; dual-quaternion skinning as a separate opt-in path never substituted by default

## Summary

Deformation state on the CPU side with upstream's exact math and public observations.

## Background (plan §7.1 "Skeletal deformation", §7.2, §5.12 Animation row, §14.9 combination "skinning+morphs+shadows+export")

"Skeletal deformation: the reference application's matrix-based skinning by default." "Dual-quaternion skinning similarly belongs in a separate opt-in path. It does not in general produce the same deformation as linear matrix blending, so substituting it by default would violate the core purpose of this project."

## Technical approach

- Bone hierarchy inside the packed transforms (06.2); `Skeleton.update()` semantics (bone inverses, `boneMatrices` array identity, `boneTexture` layout/size rules as pinned) reproduced with public array identity preserved.
- Morph targets: `morphTargetInfluences` arrays, relative morphs, morph texture packing as pinned.
- Retain `SkeletonUtils`, `CCDIKSolver`, `MMD` helpers as retained JS with tests.
- Opt-in DQ path with its own tests and a label in the report.

## Success criteria

- Upstream tests pass; differential pose tests; combination test skinning+morphs+shadows+export (with F3D-14/19) scheduled in 18b.2.

## Test plan

- Unit: bone-matrix computation tests bit-for-bit vs upstream for scripted poses; `boneMatrices`/`boneTexture` identity and layout tests; morph influence and relative-morph tests; DQ path tests behind the opt-in flag only.
- E2E: `tests/e2e/animation/skinning.mjs` on skinned examples and H7's CPU-side skeleton state on both browsers; retargeting (`SkeletonUtils`) and IK (`CCDIKSolver`) examples through the routed build; mapped upstream tests green.
- Logging: per-update `metric` events `{bones, morphs, skeleton_generation}`; mismatch events with bone name and matrices; archived under `evidence/13.2/`.
- Failure artifacts: bone matrix dumps.

## Considerations

- Skeleton generation participates in pose-cache keys (13.1) and in H7's per-instance data (16.5).
acceptance_criteria: Skeleton/skin/morph manifest records have owners and positive tests; bone matrix computation matches upstream bit-for-bit for scripted poses; morph weights/relative morphs match; retargeting/IK utilities work through the routed build; a dual-quaternion path exists only behind an explicit opt-in and is excluded from equivalence scoring by default.

title: Math family closure (every math and addon numeric utility owned and tested)
description:
## Full scope

Math family closure: every vector, matrix, quaternion, Euler, color/color-management, bounds, ray, plane, triangle, interpolant, coordinate and MathUtils operation; addon OBB/capsule/noise/hull/octree/sampling/LUT utilities; edge cases, coercions, mutability and return identity

## Summary

Close the scalar math surface completely, mostly by retaining and testing.

## Background (plan §5.12 "Math and numeric helpers", §14.9)

"Retained reference-compatible scalar surface; safe Rust bulk kernels when proven; edge cases, coercions, mutability, return identity." "Every existing callable/option/behavior family... an executable positive case... Constructor existence, identical function names, or merely retaining source bytes is insufficient."

## Technical approach

- Retained upstream math modules remain the public owners; where 06.1 kernels exist they are used only inside islands.
- Generate the family test list from the manifest; for each record write/derive a positive test (many come from upstream unit tests; fill gaps for untested methods, coercion inputs like strings/undefined, NaN handling, chained `return this`).
- Addon utilities (`OBB`, `Capsule`, `ImprovedNoise`/`SimplexNoise`, `ConvexHull`, `Octree`, `MeshSurfaceSampler`, `LUT*` loaders' math parts) retained and tested.

## Success criteria

- Manifest status for the family: all records `retained`+tested or `new-rust`+tested; upstream math tests green.

## Test plan

- Unit: the generated family suite (one positive test per manifest record with invalid-input, mutation, serialization and `return this` identity cases); mapped upstream math unit tests; kernel-vs-retained differential tests where 06.1 kernels are used.
- E2E: browser run of the family suite on both browsers (some math behavior differs by engine for transcendentals; 06.1's policy applies).
- Logging: per-record status updates `{record, owner, test, result}` feeding the manifest; archived under `evidence/13.3/`.
- Failure artifacts: the failing record's inputs and both outputs.

## Considerations

- No coverage percentage headline; per-family counts only.
acceptance_criteria: Every math-family manifest record has an owner (retained reference-compatible scalar surface by default; Rust kernel where proven and used) and a positive behavioral test including invalid-input, mutation, serialization and identity cases; return identity (methods returning this) and mutability semantics match; upstream math unit tests pass through the routed build.

title: Geometry and attributes family closure (incl. GLBufferAttribute on exact GL)
description:
## Full scope

Geometry and attributes family closure: every core/addon geometry class, indexed/non-indexed/interleaved/instanced/normalized/integer attributes, groups and draw ranges, bounds/normals/tangents computation, morph attributes, buffer update/copy/resize behavior; GLBufferAttribute using a real GL buffer on the exact route

## Summary

Close the geometry surface with the native data path and honest exact-route handling.

## Background (plan §5.12 "Geometry and attributes", §5.8, §14.9 "GLBufferAttribute behavior")

"Native data path plus retained constructors/utilities; actual GLBufferAttribute use on exact GL route, not a dummy buffer."

## Technical approach

- All `*Geometry` constructors retained (they are CPU generators) with their outputs flowing into the attribute system (06.6); every attribute kind mapped to layout rules (normalized/integer interpretation, interleaved strides) in the vertex layout keys (08.1).
- `computeVertexNormals`/`computeTangents`/bounds retained or kernel-backed with differential tests.
- `GLBufferAttribute`: only meaningful with a real GL context; the exact route must consume the user's buffer; the new backend reports it as an intrinsic native contract for that geometry (connected group, 04.4).

## Success criteria

- Family suite green; GLBufferAttribute test with a real GL buffer on the exact lane.

## Test plan

- Unit: generated family suite per geometry/attribute record (constructors, attribute kinds, groups/draw ranges, bounds/normals/tangents, morph attributes, update/copy/resize identity rules) with a Node oracle; vertex-layout key tests for every attribute kind.
- E2E: browser family suite in the functional and forced lanes on both browsers; `GLBufferAttribute` test with a real user-created `WebGLBuffer` in the exact lane.
- Logging: per-record status updates and layout-key dumps; archived under `evidence/13.4/`.
- Failure artifacts: attribute array diffs.

## Considerations

- Resize semantics (new array identity) and `copy`/`clone` identity rules are part of the positive tests.
acceptance_criteria: Every geometry/attribute manifest record has an owner and positive tests; the native data path (packed replicas + attribute histories) covers all attribute kinds; GLBufferAttribute works with a user-provided WebGLBuffer on the exact GL route and is never given a dummy buffer; upstream geometry tests pass.

title: Curves, shapes and modifiers closure (NURBS, extrusion/text, modifiers, CSG)
description:
## Full scope

Curves, shapes and modifiers closure: all paths/curves, NURBS, shape holes/triangulation, extrusion/text/fonts, geometry generators, subdivision/simplification/tessellation/curve modifiers and official CSG integrations; complete algorithms retained first, measured kernels later; topology, attributes and synchronous results preserved

## Summary

Retain the complete algorithm inventory; accelerate only what measurement justifies.

## Background (plan §5.12 "Curves, shapes and modifiers")

"Retain complete algorithms first; accelerate measured kernels; preserve topology, attributes and synchronous results."

## Technical approach

- Retained modules with generated positive tests (including degenerate shapes, holes, self-intersections as upstream handles them, font glyph edge cases).
- Optional kernel candidates recorded (triangulation, extrusion) with a rule: bit-identical topology required.

## Success criteria

- Family suite green; manifest updated.

## Test plan

- Unit: generated family suite (paths/curves/NURBS/shape holes/triangulation/extrusion/text with fonts/generators/modifiers/CSG integrations) with geometry snapshots vs a Node oracle, including degenerate shapes, holes and self-intersections as upstream handles them; kernel candidates require bit-identical topology tests.
- E2E: browser family suite on both browsers; relevant upstream examples through the routed build.
- Logging: per-record status updates; topology/attribute-order diffs on mismatch; archived under `evidence/13.5/`.
- Failure artifacts: geometry dumps.

## Considerations

- Third-party CSG/engine integrations keep their versions and semantics (§5.14).
acceptance_criteria: Every curve/shape/modifier manifest record (including NURBS utilities, ShapeUtils triangulation, ExtrudeGeometry/TextGeometry with FontLoader fonts, SubdivisionModifier, SimplifyModifier, TessellateModifier, CurveModifier, official CSG example integrations) has a retained owner with positive tests; any later kernel acceleration keeps identical topology/attribute order and synchronous results.

title: Scene graph and core data family closure (JSON, disposal/reuse, subclass and reentry)
description:
## Full scope

Scene graph and core data family closure: Object3D/Scene/Group, hierarchy/layers/visibility, EventDispatcher events, cloning, JSON serialization/deserialization (ObjectLoader), userData, manual matrix flags, traversal helpers, disposal/reuse, CPU and GPU resource observations, subclass and reentry behavior

## Summary

Close the object model with versioned packed replicas behind the JS semantic objects.

## Background (plan §5.12 "Scene graph and core data", §5.9, §5.2)

"JS semantic objects with versioned packed replicas; include subclass and reentry behavior." "Disposal releases a residency, not necessarily the public object... A legal reused material, texture, or geometry receives fresh backend residency without changing its existing JavaScript identity."

## Technical approach

- Positive tests generated per record; residency tests: dispose then reuse a geometry/material/texture and assert fresh GPU residency with the same JS object; renderer shutdown vs user disposal vs cache eviction vs device loss distinguished (with F3D-07.1 states).
- Traversal helpers (`traverse`, `traverseVisible`, `getObjectByName`) retained and covered.

## Success criteria

- Family suite green; residency/reuse tests pass in the forced lane.

## Test plan

- Unit: generated family suite (Object3D/Scene/Group, layers/visibility, events, cloning, JSON via ObjectLoader round trips, userData, manual matrix flags, traversal, disposal/reuse, subclass and reentry); residency tests (dispose then reuse a geometry/material/texture keeps JS identity and gets fresh residency; shutdown vs user disposal vs cache eviction vs device loss distinguished).
- E2E: browser family suite in the functional and forced lanes on both browsers; mapped upstream core tests green.
- Logging: per-record status updates; residency events `{object, event, generation}`; archived under `evidence/13.6/`.
- Failure artifacts: JSON round-trip diffs.

## Considerations

- Automatic deduplication must not merge observable ownership or events (§5.9).
acceptance_criteria: Every scene-graph/core manifest record has an owner and positive tests including subclass overrides and reentrant use; JSON round trips through ObjectLoader match upstream; disposal releases residencies without changing public identity and legal reuse works; upstream core tests pass.

title: Procedural geometry kernels beyond marching cubes and the GPU-generation legality rule
description:
## Full scope

Procedural geometry kernels beyond marching cubes and the GPU-generation legality rule: recognized addon generators lowered to safe Rust with identical outputs; GPU generation permitted only where output order, precision, topology, bounds and synchronous observations still satisfy the contract; physics-engine state never altered by rendering optimization

## Summary

Extend the H2 approach to other recognized generators, with the GPU rule written down.

## Background (plan §7.7)

"Start procedural geometry with known addon implementations such as marching cubes... GPU generation is valuable only where output order, precision, topology, bounds, and synchronous observations can still satisfy the contract. Rendering optimization must not change a physics engine's authoritative time step, solver iterations, simulation precision, or state."

## Technical approach

- Inventory generators reached by the corpus/held-out apps (for example terrain noise, water surfaces, particle emitters on CPU); lower the recognized ones; keep the rest retained.
- GPU legality rule document + tests (a generator whose output is read on the CPU stays CPU).

## Success criteria

- Lowered generators bit-identical; rule enforced.

## Test plan

- Unit: per-generator differential tests vs the retained addon (bit-identical outputs); GPU-legality rule tests (a generator whose output is read on the CPU is refused GPU generation); a physics-state invariance test (kernel runs leave wrapper state untouched).
- E2E: examples using the lowered generators through the routed build on both browsers with trace equality.
- Logging: per-generator `{generator, lowered|retained, reason}` and output diffs on failure; archived under `evidence/13.7/`.
- Failure artifacts: array diffs.

## Considerations

- Keep within budget; do not chase every addon generator if unused by any corpus/held-out app (record the gap as retained, tested).
acceptance_criteria: At least the procedural generators used by the corpus and held-out apps beyond MarchingCubes have kernel lowerings with bit-identical outputs, or are explicitly retained with reasons; a written legality rule governs GPU generation and is enforced by tests; no kernel modifies a physics wrapper's authoritative state.

title: H3 and H5 end-to-end routes and measured throughput
description:
## Full scope

H3 (webgl_animation_multiple) and H5 (webgl_instancing_dynamic) end-to-end routes: automatic transformation, equivalence, and measured completed-frame throughput under the frozen protocol on available strata, published as held-out-style results

## Summary

Two more headline cells, measured the same way as H1/H2.

## Background (plan §15.2 H3/H5, §16.8)

H3: "Batched animation, interpolation, transforms, shared invariant data." H5: "Update-kernel compilation and upload efficiency rather than naive instancing claims."

## Technical approach

- Same pipeline as 11.1/11.2; reference configurations from 03.3 extended to H3/H5 (R1 recipe applied; frozen before candidate runs).
